posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
🎙️ Ep. 61 of A guy with a scarf is out, with Julie Neenan Souza Souza, six years Global Head of Sports at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and now Executive in Residence at PwC.
Julie is someone I wanted on the show for a long time. While she carried the AWS badge it was never the right moment, and it got easier once she stepped away, which turned out to be the better version anyway, because the conversation went where it wanted to go, from a scrappy college sports startup to whether AI is making the next generation duller. We crossed paths at a lot of events over those years and I always admired the energy, and that on stage she brought her whole self, humour and opinions included, which is rare for someone carrying a badge that size.

Key points and quotes:
🪣 The three-bucket test for any technology project: the business problem, the solution deployed, and the outcome with a number on it. "If we can't explain it in three big buckets, then there's not a story there."
🕶️ The metaverse locker room a team asked AWS to build, and her first question: "Why do you want to do that?" She is seeing "we want an AI strategy" land in exactly the same shape now.
⏳ On measuring too early: "If you're looking for quick wins, you might have a few of those, but I don't think then you're using it to its full power either." The NFL kickoff rule was run through 10,000 simulated seasons before it changed.
🏈 "When I was at AWS, I wanted the big thorny problems."
🤝 On who should hold a multi-vendor solution together: "You want somebody you trust quarterbacking that." And on doing it all in-house: "If anybody's telling you they can do it all, that's probably not true."
🏁 On the argument that regulation means falling behind in the global race: "What are we racing toward? Like human extinction? Because I'm fine falling behind on that."
🧠 On AI and junior jobs: "How you know to make high judgment decisions is through experience." Stanford's August 2026 data has 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed jobs 19% behind their peers, with no gap for experienced workers.
🥱 On offloading your thinking to an agent: "I think you're going to be a more boring person."
🏟️ "I don't think live sports can be disintermediated."
And boy do I agree with that!!!

Full conversation in the video, companion article below.

⚽ The season on YouTube so far: 106 days
Since 1 July the 101 club and league channels of Europe’s five big leagues have published 21,001 videos and collected 2.86 billion views. I took the YouTube Football Tracker’s season dashboards apart one chart at a time, for all five leagues together and for each league on its own, and published the six pages on my research hub.

📊 All five leagues
The Premier League has 1.1 billion views from 4,287 videos, La Liga 920 million from 6,626, so the league that publishes most earns second most, and an English upload is worth three and a half times an Italian one. Shorts carry every league, from 59% of views in England to 75% in France, and the shortest Shorts and the shortest long-form clips earn the most per video everywhere.
🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 The Premier League
The league channel sets the pace with Shorts that average close to a million views, Manchester City owns long-form at 745 thousand a video, and the five most consistent channels are the five biggest. A Brighton Short with 6.3 million views and 35 comments asks a question of its own.
🇪🇸 LALIGA
Barcelona and Real Madrid take 58% of the views, the league channel owns long-form, and Sevilla gets 96% of its views from Shorts. One Alavés Short is 79% of the club’s season, and Rayo Vallecano has published 22 videos in 106 days.
🇩🇪 Bundesliga
Bayern takes almost half of all Bundesliga views from fewer videos than the league channel, the clubs stream more than any other league and get the least for it, and the biggest video of the season is a referee’s microphone. The smaller clubs win on engagement, publish on the night and vanish for weeks at a time.
🇮🇹 Lega Serie A
Juventus sets the pace on Shorts, the league channel owns long-form, Inter publishes more than anyone and gets less per video, and Napoli goes silent for most of the season. One Como Short is the only one-hit wonder in the whole league.
🇫🇷 Ligue 1
PSG takes 70% of the views and the whole of the top eleven, with one eight-second Short at 44 million views, the league channel owns long-form, and nine clubs are silent on more than half the days of the season.

👉 All six pages: https://lnkd.in/dNUg7YHp

📺 The data comes from the YouTube Football Tracker, which follows more than 100 club and league channels every night.
 ⚽ If you run social for a club or a league, it shows you what your rivals publish, when and in which format, and which of their videos actually travel.
 ✒️ If you are a sports journalist, it shows you which stories, clubs and formats are working on YouTube this week, with the numbers to back the piece.
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dTQqMGYJ

Euroleague Basketball is hiring a Streaming & Media Technology Director in Barcelona, which I spotted in David Cushnan's Leaders newsletter, and I'm sharing it because a few of the tech and ops people in my network could do this job well.

You'd own EuroLeague TV from ingest and encoding through CDN, DRM and playback, plus the media asset management, the automated content stack, the archive, content protection, geo-blocking and entitlements, onboarding of third-party content, distribution to partner platforms and the game-night incident process, with nobody reporting to you and the commercial side of partner deals handled by someone else.
If one of you gets the job, you owe me a dinner in Barcelona.
https://lnkd.in/dRdV3FCN

P.S.
A note for whoever wrote the posting, with respect, because the role is described in a lot of detail. One of the requirements is being able to write clear technical requirements and then check what vendors deliver against them, so I read the page that way and couldn't find anything on Euroleague's side: no salary range, no package, no benefits, no word on hybrid, and the page goes from "Your mission" and "Your profile" straight to "About us". That's twenty bullets of responsibilities for a Director role and nothing about what you get back, and the good candidates will ask about that in the first call anyway.

📺📲 Dolby OptiView at IBC 2026, three interviews and one booth tour.

I spent three days on the stand in Hall 5 with a microphone and a camera, and this is what the company brought to Amsterdam, in the order the demos ran:
🧠 Sports Intelligence, new. Two halves: content intelligence scores every moment of a game for excitement and cuts the clips, viewer intelligence reads the audience and predicts, minute by minute, when a fan is about to leave.
📺 Dolby OptiView Ads cut loose from the player. It now ships as an SDK that works with any player, so you keep what you run and add the ads piece.
🤝 Google Ad Manager certification, which Dolby’s release calls the first server-guided ad insertion solution verified within the Google ecosystem. Dolby’s own figure from one deployment: 76% average eCPM lift, 132% average fill-rate lift.
🎨 Dolby Vision through Dolby OptiView for the first time, with one-button up-conversion for the SDR productions that still make up most of live sport. The Seattle Seahawks are first.
⏱️ Latency as a setting, with synchronised playback across the audience.

The three people who built it walked me through it on camera:
🎙️ Giles Baker, SVP Dolby Cloud Solutions, on the strategy and the three-year view
 🎙️ Dan Coffey, Director of Product, on the portfolio and the clipping demo, recorded at 8am because the day before the booth was too crowded to film in
 🎙️ Paul Boustead, VP of Product Strategy, on exit risk and the case for lean-back personalisation

I also wrote down what I would push back on, because a sponsored stand is a captive audience and the questions a buyer should ask are harder than the ones I asked on camera.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
Netflix has bought the 2030 World Cup for Spain and Andorra, announced today with FIFA, and it will stream all 104 matches live, with one match per matchday free and a package with every Spain game, both semi-finals and the final going to a Spanish free-to-air channel that hasn’t been named yet.

I started in this business in 1987 and I have lost count of the times we said a streamer would never buy the biggest tournament in the world, in a country where football sits next to religion, and we said it with the same confidence we used for “nobody will watch a full match on a phone”. It happened anyway, the way most of those things happened, and it has a name, it’s called transformation.

Maybe Netflix is buying events and leaving league seasons to others, so the Serie A and Ligue 1 tenders he expects in the coming months probably won’t get a Netflix bid.
The free-to-air channel that gets the Spain package will be buying the national team from Netflix, and Netflix now decides what Spanish fans see for free during a home World Cup, which is a big shift for the Spanish TV market.

posts.text:
🛑 STOP Making This Mistake with Your API Strategy
I am sharing this because it truly resonates with my direct experience in streaming as a B2B vendor.

📺 Any streaming service that reaches some scale ends up living on a long list of devices, web, iOS, Android, Apple TV, Android TV, Fire TV, Roku, Samsung, LG, and the list grows with every distribution deal. Each of those apps is often built by a different team or partner, sometimes in a different language, and each one tends to carry its own copy of the rules the business runs on: who is entitled to what, which offer appears where, what happens when a subscription lapses, how a geo restriction applies to a given match. Those copies drift apart over time, so a fix lands on one platform weeks before it reaches another, and the product team spends a lot of its energy keeping ten apps in agreement with each other.

In the first clip from my conversation with Stephen Tallent, CEO of Mercury Intermedia, he goes straight at this:

 ⚙️ "So we feel it's pretty important to plan from the beginning to have all your platforms talking to the same APIs and provide as much of the business logic as possible there and really let the clients focus on the pixels. Let them focus on taking their time to make it look the way it needs to look, make it feel the way it needs to feel, making sure that user experience is great, and try to unify as much of the business logic as possible outside of the client, which saves time in some areas, takes a little longer in other areas. Again, if you plan for it, it can be done properly."

 📶 "Let the clients focus on the pixels" is the line I keep coming back to, because it gives the design and app teams back the work only they can do, how the thing feels on a 65-inch TV and on a phone on the bus, and it puts the rules that make money in one place where they get changed once. I also like that he names the cost, since some work gets slower and the payoff only comes if you decide it on day one, which is the exact decision most services skip when they are racing to get onto the next device.

 😎 Full disclosure, Mercury is a current client of A Guy With A Scarf.
The full episode is on the A Guy With A Scarf YouTube channel: https://lnkd.in/dqHguVBw
If your service runs on eight or more devices, where does your business logic live today, and how many copies of it are there?

 👉 If you want to see how Quicksilver Stream puts this into practice, ask Mercury for a demo here: https://lnkd.in/dNd9UC8R

Day one of Wave by Vento at OGR Torino, from the front row of Sala Fucine.
Tim Berners-Lee said out loud that he has no fix yet for what AI answers do to the click, the visit and the economics of publishing.
Jony Ive explained why the man who put multi-touch in every pocket gave the Ferrari Luce real analogue needles and physical controls, and admitted the launch reaction taught him that "you can make something new and different, that's rubbish, that's very easy".
Kalshi's Luana Lopes Lara told us CNN, Fox, CNBC and CBS now run her odds instead of polls.
Petar Veličković of Google DeepMind and Giorgio Chiellini agreed that a model can tell you a goal was likely and still cannot tell you why it happened, which is what coaches are paid for. Beeple brought a robot dog that squats and prints what it sees.
A strong lineup, and I wrote it all up with quotes and photos. I also wrote what made me uncomfortable as a Torinese: an opening that cast the Agnelli family as disruptors, a requested standing ovation for the host, a moderator from a paper his holding company owns, and reserved front rows while the press stood at the back. I stood up for Berners-Lee. As far as I could see, I was the only one.

▶️ A guy with a scarf NEW EPISODE
Could you run an in-house streaming platform without building every piece of it yourself, and swap an authentication, video or analytics vendor without touching a single client app?

🎙️ That is the question behind my conversation with Stephen Tallent, who founded Mercury Intermedia in 1996 and carries the CEO and CTO roles together. Mercury is a client of mine, so read this with that in mind, and I can vouch for what I saw on screen and what he said on the record.

1️⃣ Control of the endpoints your apps talk to. Stephen prefers the word control to ownership, and Quicksilver Stream keeps the business logic in one set of APIs so the apps can "focus on the pixels". His example is an authentication SDK dropped into every client app, which saves time on day one and lands the change in every app at once the day that vendor gets acquired.
2️⃣ No lock-in, including to Mercury. I challenged a vendor for saying it, and his answer was "if you provide a good product and you provide good service, they're gonna stay with you whether they have to or not". Customers keep their data, can swap any piece of the stack and can bring development in-house, which Stephen says a dozen customers have done with Mercury. He also named the tension himself: the customer needs control and the vendor needs to make money.
3️⃣ A producer builds a page by asking for it, no box-ticking and menu-scrolling. In the demo I described a feature I wanted, a producer testing a new page layout in plain language, and the team did it in front of me on the working platform. I had thought my idea was clever and it already existed, so I felt a mix of embarrassment and surprise.
One of the most clever use of AI I have seen in a B2B product so far. Great news for streaming platform producer teams.

What intrigued me about Quicksilver Stream is that it is not yet-another-streaming-platform. It sits between the client apps and the vendors a customer chooses, so video platform, or an authentication provider can change underneath it.
This conversation exists because the Mercury team read two of my articles, and one sentence in the second, "the stack is the product", led to a phone call with Tom Richardson, some strategy work together and now this interview. I write nearly every day and rarely see where a piece ends up, so for anyone asking what writing on LinkedIn returns, this is one of the clearest answers I have.

The full conversation, with the quotes and three questions to take to your own architecture, is in the article and YouTube video or Spotify podcast.

To see Quicksilver Stream, visit mercury.io and schedule a demo, and if you would like an introduction, write to me and tell me what you want to see.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
10 Things To Consider about the second Genius Sports CEO letter 📝
In March I wrote about Mark Locke's first letter, the one defending the $1.2 billion Legend deal. Seven months later there is a second one, "Americans are Going to Keep Wagering", and this time the subject is prediction markets. Same format, same footnotes, same forward-looking statements notice at the bottom, and the same audience: investors asking what happens to Genius if the courts or Congress take sports contracts away from Kalshi and Polymarket.

His point in one sentence 🎯 Americans will keep wagering on sport whatever the courts decide, and Genius gets paid however that wagering is routed, because it supplies the exchanges, the market makers behind them and the sportsbooks competing with them for the same customer. The rules decide who pays Genius; the demand, in his telling, guarantees that someone does.

The 🔟 things to consider:
1️⃣ It is an investor document that happens to be on LinkedIn, written while the Kalshi cases and the Supreme Court petition are still open.
2️⃣ The thesis separates the demand for wagering from the structure that carries it, and never describes a scenario in which Genius loses.
3️⃣ Settlement is where he is strongest: the Western Michigan at Michigan market on 5 September, $18.6 million paid out on a broadcast clock that had one second put back.
4️⃣ The economics claim, that an exchange dollar pays Genius as well as a sportsbook dollar, "match or exceed" in his words, has no public number under it.
5️⃣ Two Eilers & Krejcik percentages, 69 per cent and 2 per cent, carry the whole "net benefit" argument, and DraftKings and FanDuel read the same monitor.
6️⃣ The politics paragraph names Donald Trump Jr. and Stephanie Cutter in the same breath as a bipartisan bill to ban the contracts, which is more candid than the format usually allows.
7️⃣ Connecticut's subpoenas have two Genius entities on the list, and the letter gets past that in two sentences.
8️⃣ The February letter and this one are one argument in two parts, and Prediction.com launched two days later to prove it.
9️⃣ The timing tells you what the letter is for: after Q2, after the exchange deals, in the first NFL season with real exchange volume, built to be quoted back in a year.
🔟 What is missing: Sportradar, the leagues, the taxes already in force in Illinois and coming in North Carolina, and anywhere outside the US.

For paid members there is an appendix 📎 with the company timeline from Betgenius in 2001 to Prediction.com, four years of financials with the three 2026 guidance revisions side by side, the Legend deal terms, and a short Mark Locke bio built only on what I could source.

Do you buy the settlement argument, and would you believe "match or exceed" before seeing a number? Share what you think 👇

⚽ 🤖 FIFA wants fan journey tech for the Women’s World Cup 2027, next-generation wearables and connected substitution boards.

Earlier this year, at the Bundesliga SportsInnovation event in Düsseldorf, I shared a stage with Nicolas Evans from FIFA, talking 3D data, officiating and the Football Technology Centre, and what stayed with me was how much of FIFA's innovation work now runs through structured channels rather than conversations in a hospitality box.

This week those channels opened three new doors. The FIFA Innovation Programme has published three challenges:
⚽ Fan journey technology for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 in Brazil, which FIFA says is its first innovation challenge tied to a specific competition. Applications close on 1 November 2026, and the criteria ask for a fully operational solution already delivered across multiple projects, commercial partner integration and measurable ROI. Four weeks is short, but count backwards from kick-off on 24 June 2027 through FIFA's five-step process and there is little other room to deploy anything.
⚽ Next-generation sports wearables, measuring hydration, load, recovery and stress in real time. Working prototype minimum, no deadline, with validation through FIFA's research partners and academic institutions on offer.
⚽ Connected substitution boards, hardware that links to the substitution software FIFA already runs and shows player numbers to the stadium. Lightweight, durable, three hours of battery, manual fallback, working prototype minimum, no deadline.

All three go through the same portal, which runs on a video pitch platform, so expect to pitch on camera.

If you run fan journey, ticketing, accessibility or in-stadium technology that is already live with reputable clients, the Women's World Cup brief is written for you and the clock is running, so apply. If you build wearables or match operations hardware, the other two are open with no deadline, so get your prototype evidence in order and go. Know a company that fits one of the three? Tag them below.

And if you are preparing an application and want a second pair of eyes on the pitch, the positioning or the ROI story, message me.

Hat tip to Juan Iraola, whose post is where I first saw the announcement.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
Fanatics Betting & Gaming's CTO on Building a Sportsbook With AI
Ian Botts in conversation with Nick Meacham (SportsPro CEO) at SportsPro AI and Tech 2026

Ian Botts runs technology for Fanatics Betting & Gaming, about 920 engineers by his count, gave the funniest, which at an AI conference at 9:30 is a public service.

My take: he did the rollout in the right order, and almost nobody does. AI went inside the tools people already used, then a platform made the model a swappable part, and only after that did agents go in front of customers. The usual conference version starts with the customer-facing demo and ends with a slide.

A few lines worth keeping:
"What problem am I trying to solve?" His answer when the industry told everyone to adopt AI.
"I'm nothing but Claude from here to eternity," followed a breath later by "who knows what's going to happen tomorrow." Which is why he built the platform model-agnostic.
"Engineers are problem solvers. Writing code is a very small part of building software that is either at scale, works correctly, or God forbid, is actually secure."
And on his own coding: he has not shipped production code in a decade, and was asked to stop when it got bad.

The full piece on A guy with a scarf covers:
🤖 The sportsbook as a spreadsheet, and why Fanatics bets on FanCash instead of bonuses
🤖 The adoption numbers (4.7 days a week for engineers) and what they do and do not tell you
🤖 Meemaw and Daisy, the two agents in production, one beside support staff and one building bet slips in chat
🤖 Fuel, the reuse library behind a prediction market built in 100 days
🤖 My reservation about measuring habit instead of outcomes

Paid subscribers also get the appendices: Fanatics' three businesses with 2024 revenue by segment, the financials I could source and the ones I could not, a timeline from GSI Commerce to Ontario, and Ian's bio. Those took longer to check than the article took to write.

quoted_post.text:
🤖 What a Broadcaster, a Content Platform and a Video Infrastructure Vendor Say About Building a Sports Media Stack for AI

Sean Hunter of Fox, Daniel Kirschner of Greenfly and Chris Wilson of MediaKind on the panel I moderated at SportsPro AI and Tech 2026.

Yesterday I noticed a lot of sports people explaining AI and a lot of AI people explaining sports, so I picked a broadcaster, a content operations platform and a video infrastructure vendor and asked each to stay in their own field.
Sean said the data team at Fox now works directly with journalists and commentators, and data scientists "exist in greater numbers even than before." Fox shipped an ElevenLabs feature for the World Cup where fans put questions to Colin Cowherd, a "catch me up with the highlights" video pipeline, and announced agentic ad buying at Cannes Lions. His warning on AI features: "if you just sort of stick a chat box onto an existing product, no one knows what that's for."
Daniel, on the idea that AI makes building easier: "you can build a lot more and a lot more complex things and a lot more effective things." He compared it to spreadsheets, which people expected to end accountants. Greenfly says 25,000 athletes use its app. His view of Europe against the US: Europe asks where to store content, and the US asks how to make money on it.
Chris described how MediaKind, now combined with Harmonic, exposes its platform through MCP so that "Greenfly can plug in their agent and drive our video pipe," and Fox can do the same. On the pace of change: "Some of those models will not be here in three months," so the value is in being able to swap them and fail fast.
I closed on a sour note, since nobody has cracked fan engagement yet. Daniel's reply: "I don't think it's a solvable problem." Sean agreed. And everyone means something different when they say fan engagement.

A guy with a scarf

On the pace of change: "Some of those models will not be here in three months," so the value is in being able to swap them and fail fast.
I closed on a sour note, since nobody has cracked fan engagement yet. Daniel's reply: "I don't think it's a solvable problem." Sean agreed. And everyone means something different when they say fan engagement.

posts.text: SportsPro AI + Tech 2026: what sport is getting back from AI

quoted_post.author: Carlo De Marchis
quoted_post.text:
I spent day one of SportsPro AI + Tech at London Stadium and posted notes from the floor all day.
A question I asked myself on the way out: have I learned something new?
Meh, not really. But do I have a better understanding of what our ecosystem is doing in AI and tech, what people are thinking, trying, doing, succeeding at and failing at? Definitely yes.
So, a good day for me.

The sessions worth remembering were the ones where somebody said what didn’t work, why they stopped, or how long it took before anything paid off.
I appreciate those who put the people involved at the centre of any solution, not in a romantic way, but because, as with every process, if people are not properly on board, the results are rarely positive.
I say this with humility and respect (as someone who wanders around town with the laptop open in his hands, because there is always a Claude Code session running): sometimes it felt like people from Sports were “lecturing” us about AI, and people from the AI world were explaining sport to us. I guess it’s a very human (not artificial) way of reassuring the audience that they get it, when in reality they are just starting a journey. No need for that. Let’s all do something more useful: let’s double down on what we are experts in (if anything, in my case) and share what we have learned, including what failed, and the half-formed ideas we would bet on, so that somebody in the room holding the other half can pick them up.

One thing I observed is that we went from AI as magic, “look what I did with it”, to the “AI needs to serve a business objective” mantra, or mood.
Good. But...
The same question kept coming back on stage all day: should you start with the technology or with a business problem? I couldn’t take a position, because I think the question is wrong, or at least neither answer solves it. If I start from a business problem without knowing what the technology can now do differently, I won’t see the problem at all, since my very human brain doesn’t register something as a problem until it has a hint that it can be solved at all, and starting from the technology gives you demos and pilots that die quietly. Tech and business have to be a conversation, and I’ve lived that for most of my career: technical people need to understand the business at least well enough to know which problems are worth their time, business people need to understand the technology at least well enough to imagine what has become possible, and the two sides progress and innovate together.
😎 That is my take.

quoted_post.author: Carlo De Marchis
quoted_post.text:
🏟️ Munich wants the Olympics back. Is it a good idea?
 🇩🇪 Germany has picked Munich as its candidate for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Summer Games, reusing the 1972 Olympic Park.
I live in an Olympic city, Torino, and I'm writing this from London, where I spent three years on the digital side of the 2012 Games with LOCOG and the BBC. Right after my first Games I wrote a piece called "There is nothing like the Olympics", and I still feel the same, so when Munich was picked on Saturday I had to write about it. I also have my own memories of that stadium, including a December night in the 90s under a snow-covered roof that creaked a lot more than I liked ❄️
In the article:
 1️⃣ What Munich is proposing, and how close the vote against Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr was
 2️⃣ The 2025 referendum, and how it compares with Munich's failed 2018 and 2022 bids
 3️⃣ What reusing a 1972 park costs, starting with a €283m roof
 4️⃣ Why the broadcast operation has shrunk and is still a big job
 5️⃣ My problem with 2036, a hundred years after Berlin 1936
 6️⃣ The IOC timetable, and why Germany has to settle the year before March 2027
Thoughts?

posts.text: 10 Things To Consider after Cloudflare turned 16 and the CEO's letter

quoted_post.author: Carlo De Marchis
quoted_post.text:
10 Things To Consider after Cloudflare turned 16 and the CEO's letter

💌 Cloudflare's 2026 founders' letter, signed by CEO Matthew Prince and co-founder Michelle Zatlyn, says machines now make more requests on the web than people do, and projects 1,000 times more within five years. Here is what that means for sports media, rights holders and the vendors who sell to them.

I saw Dan Rayburn's post about the letter on Saturday night and got hooked. Some of this is technical, and I wrote it so anyone in the industry can follow.

1️⃣ The bot crossover arrived eighteen months early, and the company with the widest view of web traffic missed its own forecast by more than a year
2️⃣ Agent traffic shows up on the hosting bill first: a fan asks one question, a dozen sports sites pay to answer it, one gets the click
3️⃣ Page views were already a weak currency for sponsor reports and agents make them weaker, in both directions
4️⃣ Since 15 September, new sites with ads block AI agents by default, with separate switches for search, AI training and AI agents
5️⃣ Sports already has a pricing model for machines, in official data feeds sold to bookmakers, which most publishers are only starting to build
6️⃣ Italy and Spain made Cloudflare the villain of the piracy fight, with a €14.2 million AGCOM fine, LaLiga blocking 3,000 IPs a weekend and collateral damage on both sides
7️⃣ Agents tend to recommend whoever is already known, which is bad news for every young sports-tech vendor with a better product and a thinner footprint
8️⃣ The CEO thinks credibility will beat popularity, and the formats an agent has to cite by name are the ones that keep their value
9️⃣ A fifth of the web sits behind one company, which is convenient until it writes your crawler policy or goes down on a matchday
🔟 Cloudflare cut its "measurers" and kept building, and sports organisations are heavy on measurers

🤖 My position: treat agent access as a rights product, priced and licensed with the same seriousness as a betting feed, and tell sponsors plainly which part of the audience is people, which part is machines and which part never visited because an agent answered for them. If you are working on either of those problems, get in touch. I want to compare notes.

😁 Paid members on Substack get the companion appendix: what Cloudflare is and how it makes money, a timeline from Harvard business plan to the 2026 letter, a plain-language guide to what it sells today written for people who run sports and media businesses, and bios of Matthew Prince and Michelle Zatlyn.

posts.text:
Ben Swanton wrote this after I asked him to go deeper on a line (6.) in his IBC post, and it's worth reading if you are anywhere near a senior hire in sports and media tech.

His point is that most hiring briefs describe a job and leave out the ownership clock it is being hired into, so someone brought in during year two of a hold period to build markets and a team can struggle badly in year four, when the same title means producing a defensible growth story on a fixed timeline while half the leadership team watches for the exit.

I'd add the vendor view, because a lot of the companies selling streaming and broadcast tech are PE or VC backed and sitting somewhere on that clock, and their customers end up living with it. A sales leader hired late in a hold period gets pushed toward bookings and long contracts that read well in a data room, and the broadcaster on the other side of the table usually notices at renewal, when the roadmap conversation turns into a pricing conversation.
Ben's two questions, what has to be true in 24 months and who has to be convinced of it, are just as useful on the buying side, and I'd ask them before signing a five-year deal with any supplier.

So which clock is your main vendor running on?

quoted_post.author: Ben Swanton
quoted_post.text:
A few people picked up on the last point in my IBC post, that almost everyone is hiring to an ownership clock. Carlo De Marchis asked me to go deeper, so here it is.

I wrote recently that candidates should diligence the cap table before they sign. This is the other side of that.

Most hiring briefs describe a job. Very few describe the clock it is being hired into, and the clock usually decides whether the hire works.

Year two of a hold period and year four are different jobs with the same title. In year two you are hiring someone to build: new markets, new segments, a team that will take three years to mature. In year four you are hiring someone who can produce a clean, defensible growth story on a timeline that is already set, in a business where half the leadership team is watching for the exit. Both are legitimate. They are not the same person, and a good year-two hire can fail badly in year four.

A founder-owned business with no exit pressure can hire for a decade. A business with a strategic minority holder whose intentions are unresolved often cannot hire at all, because nobody wants to commit budget before the ownership question settles. That hesitation is itself a decision, and it usually costs more than the hire would have.

Here is what I see that most people outside the process do not. The brief a company starts with is frequently not the brief the person is eventually hired against.

That is rarely indecision. It is the clock moving. A board conversation happens, an approach arrives, a plan gets pulled forward or pushed back, and the profile shifts underneath the search. A build mandate quietly becomes a scale mandate. A regional role becomes a global one. The title stays the same and everyone carries on as though nothing changed.

Handled well, that is a good thing. A search that runs over weeks forces conversations a single planning meeting never gets to, and companies often end up hiring something better than they first described. Handled badly, the candidate is the last to know and starts the job working to a brief that expired before they signed.

The practical version: before you open a senior search, answer two questions honestly between you and your board. What has to be true about this business in 24 months, and who needs to be convinced of it. Then revisit both as the process runs, and tell the shortlist when the answers change.

If you are hiring senior commercial leadership at the moment, whose clock are you really working to?

I remember leaving that interview thinking: they are going to do something big.

I came from a completely different industry and knew very little about nuclear energy. But I immediately saw the ambition, the vision and the sense of purpose that was driving them.
 
A very special friend, Christopher Kenna, told me once that what drives me is purpose. Looking back, I think that is why saying "yes" to newcleo felt so natural.
 
Along the way, the company grew. Leadership changed, priorities evolved, milestones were reached, and new people joined the journey.
Through it all, there was always a remarkable group of people determined to keep building and believing in what we are trying to achieve.
If there is one thing I am proudest of, it is having helped bring those people together around a common story and purpose.
 
To everyone at newcleo, and to everyone who backed us when this was still a conversation in a room: thank you.
This is a huge milestone, but what makes it truly meaningful is that it brings us one step closer to the purpose that brought so many of us here in the first place.
I can't wait to see what comes next and I can’t wait to continue growing together!

I was writing a post and just noticed the infamous "Enhance Post" button that was removed is now being substituted by a more useful PROOFREAD button - see images below.

posts.text:
🔟❓Attempts to answer those 10 questions I had for IBC 2026 ⁉️
Two weeks ago I published the ten questions I was taking to IBC 2026.
I promised myself I would come back and answer every one of them, including the ones where the answer is that I still do not know.
My take on the show first: 🟩 quality over quantity, 🟩 less posturing, 🟨 fat portfolio syndrome (everybody now offers everything), and 🟨 a tough market for everyone where sport moved even further centre stage.

My 10 almost answers:
1️⃣ Market or calendar? Answered. The exceptional year raised the bar, and sport is now the workload everybody designs against.
2️⃣ DAZN eating the world? Answered, with a twist. Yes, and the DTC apps left standing are run by people who did the homework. Only the brave are left.
3️⃣ Fixing what fans complain about? Partly. Ads are moving, discovery is stuck, price is sliding, and buffering is the one I am losing hope on.
4️⃣ Fan insight reaching production? Partly, and the one I am most encouraged by. The OBS drones at Milano Cortina were built because fans asked to feel closer. That is the second case after vertical video.
5️⃣ Demo to deployment? Answered, and the answer is a new problem. AI coding shortened both paths and gave us a confused market where nobody knows which of a vendor's twelve modules is the good one.
6️⃣ AI as cover or as the job? Halfway. AI slop went front page this summer, so posturing gets spotted by everyone now, and vendors adjusted.
7️⃣ Who runs the tools? Open. Everybody says human in the loop, and the phrase covers two very different states: deliberate control, or a tool that is not ready.
8️⃣ Nobody publishes the numbers? Open, no progress. The only public metric this industry has is what survives, with a two-year lag.
9️⃣ Bottom line or top line? 75/25 by my own reading, and the 25 now comes with a serious attempt to show where the revenue comes from. Overdue.
🔟 What is the buy side buying? Open, and I will not pretend otherwise. One observation from my corner: clients came looking for innovation that makes a measurable difference, and they came prepared to evaluate it.

Four answered, three partly, three open, and the open ones are all about evidence and accountability. The tools got better, the marketing got more truthful, the buyers got more serious, and the industry still cannot show its own numbers.
If you read any of these ten differently, tell me. If you are on the buy side and can correct question 10, tell me twice.
I was there for Dolby OptiView and also represented Mercury Intermedia.

🏃‍♂️ On the day of the World Athletics Ultimate Championships I decided to launch my new athletics interactive experience.
🏃‍♀️‍➡️ The World Record Film turns the whole history of athletics records into cards you flip through — one film for the men, one for the women, 33 cards each.

🏃‍♂️‍➡️ My love for athletics started when i was a kid, Pietro Mennea, Dwight Stones, etc… then professionally in 1991 when I worked more than one year for the Tokyo World Championships and saw the magic of Carl Lewis and Mike Powell world record.

🏃 Two films — men and women, 33 cards each, in World Athletics' own event order.
📈 The staircase — every mark that ever held the record; the width of each step is how long it survived.
👻 The ghost race — press play and every era runs at once. Bolt crosses the line 9.6 m ahead of 1912.
🕳️ The pit — jumps and throws laid out at the distance they actually went, oldest at the back.
❓ Cards that explain themselves — why a ratified record sometimes goes backwards: hand timing, rule changes, a redesigned javelin.
📊 Stats for one event — nations, athletes, age and reign length, narrowed to the card you're on.
🌍 Nations — who owned each record, year by year. The USA held the 100 m for 77 of its 114 years.
🏅 Where records fall — every record as a dot, gold for the Olympics, cyan for the Worlds, grey for everywhere else. Grey wins.
📅 Records per day — all 1,382 marks on a 366-day calendar. 84.5% fall between May and September; 106 days have never produced one.
🎂 Age — how old they were, with a decade slider to watch it move.
⏳ How long records last — the longest reigns ever, each drawn from the day it was set to the day it fell.
⚖️ One ranking, men and women — every standing record in a single list. The oldest is 43 years old.
🔗 Every card has its own link — and it reloads exactly where you left off.

posts.text:
❓ What if there is another way to buy a streaming tech stack?
Own the platform, rent the expertise, keep the right to change your mind on every supplier.

🤖 I spent most of my career on the vendor side of streaming. At every renewal the same clients asked the same two questions. Can we own more of this? Can we depend on you less? I answered with contract clauses. Exit terms, data export, an escrow nobody opened. They rented, we held the keys.

📰 A few months ago I wrote about consolidation narrowing choice and ownership coming back as a buying criterion. A team in Nashville/NYC called me, read a few of my sentences back to me and said this is what we are building. That team is Mercury Intermedia. They announced Quicksilver Stream this week. I advise them, paid, so read me as interested.
What those clients were asking for, and what an in-house streaming platform gives them:

🎛️ Control. The decisions about the platform sit on the client's side of the table.💰 Investment. Fees accumulate into an asset instead of expiring with each contract.
🔌 Pluggable vendors. DRM, payments, data, ads swapped at the server side, apps untouched.
🛡️ Security. A platform that survives whatever happens to the company that built it.
📈 A long horizon. A stack that grows with the business instead of forcing a rebuild every four or five years.

The counter-arguments are real and they are in the article. Ownership without operational excellence is a marketing word. A license plus support looks like SaaS, until the vendor gets bought and only one of you keeps a platform. Control has a running cost. The price is capital, and the same buyers sign three-year SaaS deals worth more.

I understand this model may not be for everybody. It makes a lot of sense for rights holders and media brands that expect to be running their own audience relationship in ten years and want agency over the thing that runs it.

Full article below.
I am at IBC in Amsterdam from Friday to Sunday. If you want to argue any of this, or hear more, come and find me.

posts.text:
A guy with a scarf asks a question to...
Untangling MoQ with Jan Ozer

Latency is the debate that comes back every trade show and rarely gets interesting. While putting together my 10 questions for IBC 2026 I kept running into three letters, MoQ, so I asked the person I trust most on codecs and delivery, Jan Ozer, to explain what it is and why anyone in sports should care.

What Jan told me, in his words:
1️⃣ "MoQ stands for Media over QUIC. It's a new way to deliver live video over the internet with less than a second of delay, even when the audience is very large."
2️⃣ "Today, to achieve low latency in a broadcast setting, streaming platforms generally choose between two imperfect options."
3️⃣ "WebRTC provides extremely low latency and works well for interactive applications like video calls, telehealth and remote control. But WebRTC is designed primarily for two-way communication. Distributing a WebRTC stream to millions of viewers requires specialized servers and substantial infrastructure. It's too expensive for general broadcasts like the Super Bowl or the World Cup."
4️⃣ "HLS and DASH handle one-to-many broadcasting very efficiently and work well with existing content delivery networks. But even their low latency versions typically remain several seconds behind the action."
5️⃣ "MoQ is designed to fill the gap between them. It's primarily for one-to-many broadcasting, not two-way interaction."
6️⃣ "A broadcaster publishes a stream. Viewers subscribe to the stream. And relay servers distribute copies from locations close to the viewers. A relay can receive one copy of the stream and pass it to many viewers, much like a conventional content delivery network."
7️⃣ "That gives MoQ the real-time performance associated with WebRTC and the massive scale associated with HLS and DASH."
8️⃣ "The most obvious markets are live sports betting, auctions, gaming and other large events where even a few seconds of delay can spoil the experience. If your neighbor cheers before you see the goal, or the betting market changes before your video catches up, latency matters."
9️⃣ "MoQ is still an emerging standard. Products and early deployments exist, but the specification and supporting ecosystem are not yet finished."
🔟 "MoQ is not replacing WebRTC, HLS or DASH tomorrow. But it may eventually provide something the industry has always wanted: real-time one-to-many broadcasting at internet scale and affordable costs."

quoted_post.text:
Thank you to everyone who commented, wrote in privately, and suggested corrections on the AI Football Observatory over the past few weeks — a special thanks to Fabio Lalli for his constant support and advice on this initiative.

The methodology changed. It's no longer a qualitative editorial judgment: every AI initiative now gets a score based on operational status (from pilot to structural deployment) and public evidence (from a generic claim to a measured result with real numbers). Industry sources count for 60% of an official source. Each value-chain area covered adds points.

September's ranking surfaced three things I didn't expect.

Sevilla FC stays first, but not because of the brand. Its Scout Advisor, built with IBM watsonx and in production since January 2024, remains the only LLM system applied to scouting at industrial scale across the entire Observatory.

Sport Lisboa e Benfica enters the top five without ever having had a published case study before now. Twenty years of computer vision on youth development, with direct, documented ROI: João Félix, Enzo Fernández, over €240 million from two transfers alone.

Como 1907, in Serie A since 2024, outranks Milan, Inter and Juventus. Como's Kitman Labs initiative has covered the first team and Academy since last October. The three historic Italian clubs each have isolated initiatives, not yet a platform.

Six different clubs tie at the bottom of the table, each with a single verified case. It's the most honest snapshot of the market today: adoption is wide, depth isn't there yet.

Full club profiles, cited sources, score per initiative: https://lnkd.in/dsCHZgDH

I spent the last week researching LIV Golf and ended up with a quite complete deep dive which I posted in full on my Substack for the paid membership level.
I started from the filed accounts at Companies House, PIF’s own annual report, the OWGR board’s decision, the PGA Tour’s published terms, and the Financial Times reporting that broke the bankruptcy preparation. Where the published numbers disagree with each other, I have said so and shown both rather than picking the one that suits the argument. Around 10,000 words, eight appendices, every figure dated and sourced.

What's inside:
⛳ 2021-2022: buy the supply. Origins, Centurion, and the signing money, name by name.
⛳ The legal war, and the press release that ended it. The antitrust suit, the framework agreement negotiated in secret, and the three years of nothing that followed.
⛳ The audience that never showed up. The CW and Fox deals, the ratings, and the world ranking fight LIV changed its own format to win.
⛳ What worked. The majors, the Ryder Cup, and the one part of the business that did what LIV promised, the public attendance.
⛳ What the accounts say, and what LIV says. The filings against the briefings.
⛳ The fund. PIF at $913bn, its sports portfolio, and the squeeze that ended this.
⛳ 29 April 2026. The pullout, and the season coming apart in public.
⛳ 2026: the players move. The Returning Member Program, who took it, who did not.
⛳ LIV 2.0, and who pays for it. BC Partners, the prepackaged bankruptcy, and the players being asked to fund their own league.
⛳ The merger. Why it is dead, on the record.
⛳ What it bought. The three things LIV moved, including the ones the PGA Tour kept.
⛳ Appendix A: the cast. Twenty-two people, what they did, where they are.
⛳ Appendix B: who joined. Thirty-three signings with dates and reported fees.
⛳ Appendix C: who left, and where they went.
⛳ Appendix D: the teams. All thirteen, captains and rosters.
⛳ Appendix E: the tournaments. Every season, and every 2026 event with its winner.
⛳ Appendix F: the broadcast deals. From YouTube to the CW to Fox, and what each was worth.
⛳ Appendix G: the timeline. October 2021 to the bankruptcy preparation, in order.
⛳ Appendix H: attendance. What LIV published, what it did not, and the one comparison that explains the whole thing.
⛳ Sources. Fifty-one, with full links.

I am reflecting on the latest news about innovative sport properties being in trouble lately, from staff cuts up to 50% to vendors suing clients (which is a very rare thing to happen in our industry). LIV Golf Kings League Baller League etc...
I see a group of people super happy about these failures, as they predicted them in advance.
I have a lot of empathy for anybody (I mean real people) impacted negatively by these situations, unpaid wages, unpaid invoices, being laid off after having worked with passion and intent for years.
But I am still a big fan of new stuff entering our industry because they force the traditional sport giants to rethink, which very often they would not do by themselves.
External forces have brought a lot of needed innovation into what we do, even if in some cases they do not work as expected.
So for the industry as a whole it is a net positive.
Basically the big guys have an innovation department paid out by others - why do they complain about it?

Example: take football, do you think the gods of football would have implemneted any rule change if kings League did not happen? I moderated a panel pre-COVID in Germany where an ex-NFL exec was lightly joking with an ex-UEFA Gen Sec, that their football had the courage to change the rules of the game every year if they found something was off or to be improved and our football did not change anything ever.
This season, positive feedback from coaches and commentators after the first Lega Serie A matchday for effective time improvement.
I am sure many of you will disagree.

In July 1935 the US Army flew its brand new bomber, the Boeing Model 299. It crashed on take-off and killed the test pilot, one of the most experienced in the country. He had forgotten to release the lock that holds the controls still on the ground.

The verdict at the time: "too much aeroplane for one man to fly."

The fix was a card. Pilots wrote down what to check before take-off, and the aircraft went on to fly 1.8 million miles without a serious accident. We know it today as the B-17.

Checklists are made for experts. Load makes all of us forget things we know perfectly well.

Which brings me to the orange book that travelled with me this summer.
Carlo De Marchis has written "10 Things to Consider: Becoming a Better B2B Tech Vendor in Sports and Media". 200 pages, 51 working lists, built on three decades on the vendor side.

Each list is tied to a moment: before you engage a client, before you commit to a deal, when a project changes direction, when the pressure rises during delivery.

With my Broadpeak strategy hat on, four categories went straight to the top of the pile:
 - Go-to-Market Design
 - Marketing, Positioning and Market Perception
 - Partnerships and Ecosystems
 - Emerging Trends and Structural Disruption

A lot of it is what we have all learned along the way, sometimes the hard way. The value is having it packaged in a neat checklist, in order, ready to run.

Now, September is a phase transition too. Exactly the moment a pilot runs the checklist...  So, back to work. Starting with this one. 📙

posts.text:
⚽ Top 5 leagues are kicking off — football is back.
An interactive way to watch a whole season at once — and to see not just the points teams win, but the ones they let slip.

📊 So I built a little something — yet another of my sport interactive experiences.
👇 https://lnkd.in/dnsqCT9x

⚽🏈 And TBFH, to be fully honest: this is a rework of an NFL visualization I’ve been chipping away at for years — which I’ll finally launch at the start of September. This football version just… jumped the queue.

💻 I wanted one big landscape screen where I could keep all the matches of a season in view at once — every result, every club, the whole shape of a league in a single glance.
🤖 But there’s a second idea in here, and it’s not mine — it’s my son Miles’ (11), who plays for a Juventus elite academy team. He looks at the table differently - he is also a big consumer of all my interactive experiences from his iPad, with the unwanted side effect of the number of sports data and stats question from him increase dramatically, which I totally am not able to reply to.

His thinking: at the start of a Serie A season, every team already
owns all its points. 38 games × 3 = 114 points, sitting in the bank. From there you don’t earn points — you try not to lose them. Lose a match, 3 gone. Draw, you still drop 2. A tie isn’t a small win; it’s mostly points let slip.

He imagined having a physical “thing” in the locker room where the team manually moves blocks from the upcoming games to either the positive (win) or negative (lost) or both sides (tie) of the tower, maybe made with Lego?

So instead of a normal table, each team is a tower: what it kept stacks up, what it dropped pulls down — and a draw shows on both sides, because it’s +1 earned and 2 lost at the same time. Two teams on equal points can look completely different once you see the points they gave away. I call them towers as they started vertical then I also did a horiziontal version which works best on landscape, both models are available.

It’s a very simple visualization — honestly not the most visually satisfying thing I’ve made 🙂 — but it’s the best way I’ve found so far to see a season the way Miles sees it. Data updates once a day as matches are played.

My friend Gabriella Vacca knows a thing or two about managing thousand of people in a media and tech organization, and what an effective leader can do to be effective in those scenarios. Once you are running that scale of people across several countries, the "why" stops travelling through you in person and has to be built into the structure.
Values (yeah, I know,  boring...) and how you transmit them, become the vehicle for leadership.
Transparency being a key one for tech functions:
"Transparency is not, well, I'll give you access to all the reports that I have. And so, no, that's too specific for the business to really understand what it means. So you need to find the right language that can resonate with your customers."

I guess you have been in some sports and media meeting rooms - in either side - and have faced a similar situation. Have you?

❌ What clients are telling me about LinkedIn right now
Three complaints I have heard in two weeks, and why I am listening before I argue back.

I have heard a few clients commenting in a similar fashion while I have been discussing supporting and augmenting their marketing strategy, specifically for LinkedIn. So even if this is purely anecdotal and empirical, I will try to consolidate what I have heard recently.
It's their voice, not mine.

 1️⃣ "LinkedIn as a channel is becoming problematic for us. With AI, everybody is an expert on anything, posting images, visuals, PDFs and articles that are flooding the space, even when what they publish is not strictly AI slop."
 2️⃣ "So even if LinkedIn is trying to address the problem with a new algorithm and new tools, we still feel this has made it harder for us to invest effort into that platform."
 3️⃣ "The new algorithm, which may need some time to become accurate at a significant level, seems to be punishing the people and brands it was built to help."

As LinkedIn is my main channel for that line of business, this is not great to hear.
I know I should have all the right arguments to counter this, and it is also good to listen to the client side even when you may not agree 100%, and then try to restart from there.
So I do not have answers for now.
I am sure Dani Markovits may have something to say here...

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
🚗 F1 Interactive Experience
After World Cup and Tennis, my third attempt at creating an alternative experience for interactive sport. A showcase.
Live at https://lnkd.in/dksqnmgk

❓❓❓ Why
Why I am doing this?
Bottom line: I want to be hired as a dataviz creative director of a sport/media entity.
The real story: These are the kind of things I used to deisgn, build, launch, operate with the at Deltatre for many years since I started working on “the web” since 1994!!! I always loved interactive experiences for sport and I was always looking for the dataviz holy grail, which in our industry could be defined as that idea, experience, visual, or stats that you launch and is then adopted clients in sport and media and eventually by fans worldwide. So now that I can do it all by myself and pivot quickly, I decided to spend these summer months dedicating a portion of my professional time to explore.
I want to show there are alternatives to what is a standard web experience for spot websites, and regain a bit of passion in how these are done today.
❌ A web experience, when everything is social media?
I don’t have the ambition to replace official websites, some of which are good, some of which are average, some of which are style-1999 even these days, with major issues we would not be allowed to have in the 2000s and our clients would have kicked are digital-asses for.
❌ A landscape-first, when everything is vertical-mobile?
True that. Dumbest approach these days, when even athletics is moving the clock and time in the middle optimized for vertical videos. But to deep dive properly I needed a landscape model. In the end that could work well also unattended on a big screen... I even created a 1248 cards film for all World Cup players… why? I have no idea, I like wierd stuff. And did a YouTube video of that too.

🤖 How
I started playing around with the World Cup Bracket from a original design I saw online and then started making it interactive, … and then I lost control and started adding all types of visualization and interactivity. From there I did not stop.
The basic idea see if we can do two things:
The master view: Put everything on one page and make interactivity serve
The film: Create a deep dive film-style set of cards to highlight in a pre-establish order (ranking, …)
Everything is built with a simple tech stack in this case (I am doing more complex B2B stuff too) using a mix of front-end models as needed.
The programming is all done through Claude Code with extended hours of conversation and feature definitions, visual design and UX refinement.

🎛️ What
F1viz turns the 2026 season into a set of cards you flip through — one film for the Drivers, one for the Constructors, one for the Races. Every card is a small data-story you can read at a glance or dig into. This guide walks through every screen and every marker.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
🏟️ World Athletics Ultimate Championship: An Innovation Attempt - I will Be Watching on September 11-13

💾 My love for athletics. I started in this industry in 1987 and spent nearly two years living inside athletics, preparing for the 1991 World Championships in Tokyo. I worked with the federation for years after that and helped launch the first iaaf.org website.

⏱️ What you learn on that kind of build is that athletics is a multi-sport event happening in one location under one production. Multiple broadcast feeds converging on a master production that decides, second by second, which discipline goes live. Replays owed to concurrent events, moments missed because the schedule shifted, and those surreal silences...

Innovations:
🎬 Broadcast
 1️⃣ Rebuilt graphics with AR, athlete headshots and new data layers
 2️⃣ Live win probabilities and projected finishes, weighted to recent form, updated in real time
 3️⃣ Race clock moved to the bottom of the screen so the feed works vertically
 4️⃣ Fan input into the graphics design before launch
 5️⃣ A second-by-second show script, shared between broadcast and event presentation
 6️⃣ An unnamed new viewing experience, announced and not yet detailed
🏟️ Competition and presentation
 1️⃣ A black infield, with only the areas in use lit
 2️⃣ One field event at a time wherever the schedule allows
 3️⃣ Centre-court-style interviews shown in-stadium and live on the world feed
 4️⃣ A bespoke sound identity, with Mondo Duplantis delivering the Ultimate Anthem
 5️⃣ Live acts opening each warm-up, plus a full lighting rig
 6️⃣ Live lane draws for the 200m, staged the day before
🏃 Athlete experience
 1️⃣ The Day Before on 10 Sept: red carpet, media day, kids' athletics challenge led by Jefferson-Wooden and Tebogo, press conference with Coe and Bolt
 2️⃣ Footage rights reserved so athletes get video and photography of their own discipline for their own channels
 3️⃣ Tara Davis-Woodhall competing and serving as lead content creator
 4️⃣ Club Ultimate by Noah Lyles, an athlete-only after-party he helped shape
 5️⃣ No medals. A participation token for all, and a champion's trophy that connects to it
 6️⃣ Dedicated integration for athletes' families
📱 Digital
 1️⃣ A new World Athletics app: live results, stories, video, predictions, games, notifications, built to run year-round
 2️⃣ A season-long Road to the Ultimate tracker, live since 2025

📌 My take: I will be watching.
The compact format means fewer athletes and fewer events, but I focus on commercial and experiential aspects. I am curious about whether athlete footage rights become a standard term, the new broadcats format works well, the app survives to the next edition, guaranteed payment holds talent against a league offering equity, athletes will see this as a pinnacle event in their career.

📖 Full piece: sourced facts, the full innovations list, and athlete, media and fan reactions kept separate from my own reading. Link below. 👇

10 Things To Consider About Streaming the World Cup
It took me a few weeks to work out what actually happened in streaming across those six weeks. I collected a lot of sources, starting from the great work Dan Rayburn does on these occasions, and tried to distil some findings.

10 things I took from it:
1️⃣ The night streaming beat linear, once
2️⃣ Chaotic streaming audience number
3️⃣ Focus point: Brazil, YouTube and beyond
4️⃣ The delivery record from the infrastructure side
5️⃣ UHD was available at source and most rights holders declined it
6️⃣ Latency? Synchronization
7️⃣ The money came from a stoppage in play
8️⃣ Acquisition was great, what about retention?
9️⃣ Record piracy takedowns
🔟 Capacity forecast is a science, in football… a bit less

My take: we have solved the engineering, or most of it. Live sport streams at global scale now and it holds. What we do not have is any industry system to tell us how it went exactly.
Is there anybody who could enforce transparency based on a global standard for streaming stats, and do we even need one? From my partial observation point I would say yes.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
Ep. 59: Gabriella Vacca - International Executive in Telco and Streaming - Movement Is Life
What changes when your team stops being people you know by name

We studied computer engineering together in Turin, she built an international career: Olivetti, Omnitel, Bouygues Telecom, AT&T, ESPN Mobile, Gogo, ten years at Comcast, five years as CTO of Sky Italia.

Highlights from the conversation 👇
🏗️ Under 300 people the why travels through you personally. Above that you build it into the organization, using the Gartner pyramid with a values layer underneath and KPIs that serve  both the tech org and the business.
🩺 Transparency, properly defined. You get your blood test back but you don’t need a doctor simply to read your scores. You need interpretation, empathy and plain language: Am I fine? Can I get better? Should I be seriously worried? That is what the business needs from technology.
⛔ She once stopped a meeting with lawyers in the room because her own team had withheld a data point. "Please forgive us for failing to uphold our commitment to transparency”. 
🌲 Intended change is like crossing a forest that you have never crossed before. You keep the far side in view, bring the right equipment, hire the skills you do not have, and say out loud what you know and what you do not.
😴 She needs seven hours of sleep, and during COVID at Comcast that was operational data, which is why the plan started with shifts for everybody and a designated backup for every team member, including herself, so operations could continue 24/7 if anyone became unavailable.
📺 Live media changed the way her team measured performance. Once the damage is on screen, it cannot be undone, so the team tracked near misses and how often they switched to contingency.
📈 Turin taught her that risk is personal, so failure feels personal. Moving to the States rewrote that mindset into four words: “Movement is life, Movement is learning”. Be satisfied with 92%, because investing 100% of your energy in a single destination leaves every other opportunity unexplored.
🏊 "I define myself as a swimmer and not a diver." The senior leader’s job is to make sense of complexity so that others can make sound decisions, including when the right technology decision is the wrong decision for the company.
🎙️ She now hosts The Reality of Women at Work Podcast on the EveCareers Network. Her definition of luck is readiness plus opportunity, combined with the ability to actually say yes.
🧠 Three good things for every bad one, every day, because the brain latches onto the negative and must be trained to do otherwise.
Of everything we discussed, the line that stayed with me most was: "I want to be a chip in your brain. I don't want to be a line in your to-do list."

#leadership #streaming #womenatwork A guy with a scarf

posts.text:
💰 💵 💶 Now that the FIFA kerfuffle is over, the good news is we know there is a lot of capital ready to be invested in great football.

So this morning I thought, let's extract from my idea archives, or should I say "Stupid Idea Lab", what I tried hard to have someone listen to, with zero success, at the start of 2023, a month after my solo career began.
Maybe this time I will be luckier...

It's called
 ⚽ THE 3M TOURNAMENT 🇮🇹 🇪🇸 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

So the stupid idea is that I noticed that there are 3 big football cities starting with M, all with 2 great clubs, Madrid, Manchester, Milano, where the winner is the city, not the club.

1️⃣ 3-day tournament in summer
2️⃣ All clubs play each other, then 2 cities qualify for the final
3️⃣ In the final, each city fields one club for the first half and its rival for the second.

posts.text:
⚽  📺  📲 Keep fans in sync: How to ensure viewer synchronization for live sports.
I recently wrote about it and here comes a very clear explanation byt someone who is a bit more techie than me on streaming tech  😎: Jan Ozer
What he is basically saying is:

1️⃣ Measure both numbers. Track glass-to-glass latency from the pitch to the screen, and track whether every viewer sees the same play at the same moment. Report them separately.

2️⃣ Instrument drift and viewer spread. Drift is how far one viewer has slipped from the target. Viewer spread is the gap between your earliest and your latest viewer. Spread is the number to put on the dashboard.

3️⃣ Test the spoiler path. Compare your stream against a live social feed on a second device. If the feed announces the goal first, you have a synchronization defect.

4️⃣ Match the protocol to the use case. WebRTC at 0.2 to 1 second for betting and co-watch. HESP at 1 to 9 seconds for interactive sports. HLS at 9 seconds and above for broadcast-style OTT with maximum device reach. Run more than one where the audience needs it.

5️⃣ Set targetOffset deliberately. Configure the default in the dashboard or API, then override per source or per viewer in the player where you need finer control.

6️⃣ Define the drift window. Set minimumOffset and maximumOffset around the target. Inside the window the player runs at normal speed. Outside it the player adjusts playback speed by around 8% to bring the viewer back.

7️⃣ Set forceSeekOffset as the hard limit. Past that line the player performs a hard seek to the target. This is also the mechanism that holds sync on older devices with no support for fine speed adjustment.

8️⃣ Keep the window asymmetric. Defaults sit at 0.66x targetOffset behind and 1.5x ahead. Allow more room behind the target than in front of it.

9️⃣ Verify on real devices. Check the same match on phone, tablet, smart TV, and legacy player, on different networks, and record the spread across all of them.

#streaming #sportstech

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
My friends at LinkedIn News Europe asked what advice I'd give someone who wants to work across cultures. Benjamin Braun's answer in the latest Leadership Lessons is immersion. Watch the films, read the local press before you land.
😎 My story runs a different way, and so does my approach.
I never chose to work internationally. From my first day in sports production in the late 80s, it was the only environment I knew. Different countries, different languages, different ways of getting things done, every week, every month, for years on end.
Back then being multicultural started with something dull. Knowing which electrical plugs a country ran on. The logistics of producing anything abroad before digital existed. You earned respect for a place by getting the small things wrong first.
📲 Digital changed the mechanics of all of it. You read a country's press over coffee, sit in a call with a team in Seoul before lunch, share a working file across four time zones by the evening. Translation is instant. Local context is one search away. The preparation Benjamin Braun describes takes an afternoon now, where it used to take months and a shelf of paper. What digital left untouched is the time it takes for people to trust you. Tools got faster than that. Over the years I have come to know people properly through a screen. Working relationships that ran for a decade on calls, messages and shared files, with real depth in them. Then you finally meet one of those people in a hotel lobby in Doha or Munich and something else arrives, an emotion no call has ever given me.
💡 True story. Some of my biggest contracts started with a LinkedIn message from people I had stopped working with five or seven years earlier. One line, out of nowhere, from a room I had left long ago. I still have those messages saved.
We were never tourists. On a big event you might work with local partners for two, three, four years before anything happened on the field. That kind of time with people builds a connection a short visit never gives you.
🏃‍♀️ Tokyo, 1991. World Championships in athletics. We spent months there the year before, producing everything in two writing systems, Latin and Japanese, across printouts and live broadcast, all of it synchronised by hand. Pre-internet. It was the hardest and most fascinating start I could have asked for. It showed me how far a culture can sit from your own assumptions, and how much you gain by paying attention.
✅ Two words carry most of it for me. Curiosity and respect. Every so often, in a handful of rooms, I still catch a trace of old imperial habit in the way someone speaks to a local partner. Usually from people who would be mortified to hear it put that way. It quietly closes doors they never see close.

There are still things about the way I work that I cannot explain to a colleague from somewhere else, so my own work here is far from finished.

#LeadershipLessons Solange Uwimana Yessi Bello-Perez A guy with a scarf

Ep. 58: Dani Markovits - Why LinkedIn Now Measures the Person Behind the Post
The Shake Content CCO on the credibility shift, athletes moving in, and why the person now carries the brand.

I sat down with Dani Markovits for episode 58 of A guy with a scarf, summer edition. Dani was one of LinkedIn's first creator managers and spent four years there. He now runs client work at Shake Content.

🎯 People show up with intent. People open LinkedIn ready to connect and talk business. That is why the DMs work and the trust holds.
🎙️ Earn the right to go off-topic. Lead with your expertise, then add the human side. That mix is what makes a profile worth following.
🏟️ Sport is arriving late. Athletes finally see LinkedIn as the one place the audience wants to hear about the life beyond the pitch. As Dani put it, they don't want to be known only as the tennis guy or the football lady.
📊 Small audiences can win. "You don't need a huge audience." Who you get in front of is what counts.
🤖 The algorithm now checks who is posting. LinkedIn weighs whether you have the credibility to speak on a topic. The same football post travels further from me than from Dani, and that is the right call. Reach can dip. Engagement holds or climbs.
💰 LinkedIn is finally serving creators. A native creator marketplace, video monetization, a call-out feature. Brands understand that experts drive the decisions, and in B2B they all live here.
🙂 Build around the person. Only low single digits of people actually post on LinkedIn. The room to stand out is wide open.
🏢 Companies changed their minds. Four years ago firms blocked employees from posting. Now they push them and even hire on the strength of their LinkedIn activity. Brand equity flows through your own people.
📬 And after telling everyone else to do it for years, Dani launched his own newsletter, "LinkedIn/actually."

My position: LinkedIn rewarding credibility over raw reach is the healthiest move the platform has made in years. It favors people who know their subject and show up as themselves.

#linkedin #creators #content #ai

quoted_post.text:
🏁 Ep. 83: Philipp Männer, WRC Promoter - How Rally Built a Direct-to-Fan Business
Why the US is WRC's number one digital market, with no event and no local hero.

For episode 83 of Retention Zone I sat down with Philipp Männer, Senior Director Media Rights and OTT at WRC Promoter. Rally has one of the toughest live products in motorsport, and it has become a real global streaming business. Here is what stuck with me:
🎯 One role owns all of distribution. Broadcast licensing and owned-and-operated platforms under one person. Still rare, and it matches how fragmented distribution actually is now.
🏎️ The product is unique. Rally is a time trial across ~20 stages, Thursday to Sunday. WRC All Live carries every stage live, 20 to 25 hours per event. Fans behave like golf fans. Once they are in, they watch everything.
📺 Rally.TV is a service and a brand. One home for WRC and ERC, plus a FAST channel across Europe, a pay channel, and a DAZN deal.
🇺🇸 The US is WRC's number one digital market. Grown organically through digital, led by the More Than Machine doc on YouTube. An event is planned in the US in 2027.
🔁 Retention first. A fan-requested interactive data overlay just shipped, with more data and AI storytelling coming. Growth moves never come at retention's expense.
💶 Pricing is the next frontier. 13 euros a month, 120 a year today. Installments launched last August and were a big success. Localization, freemium, and flexible payments are next, market by market.
📅 Events and drivers beat seasonality. Local heroes pull their home audiences, and that matters more than the calendar for a sport this spread out.

⚽ 📺 📲 A Story About Latency and Synchronization at the FIFA World Cup 2026™ - Canada, Mexico and the United States
What multi-device viewing taught me about synchronization, latency drift, and the notification that beats the picture.
For years we have argued about latency. This World Cup handed me a different problem. Synchronization.
I watched in Italy on DAZN, across a living room, a studio and a country house. Same match, several screens, every screen sitting in its own moment. The kids' tablet ran a few seconds off the big screen. My phone, notifications on, buzzed seconds before anything happened on the television. Most of the time it was right. Someone was about to score.
Here is why. The alert fires off the live data feed the moment the goal goes in, and reaches your phone in a second or two. The picture is still crawling through encode, packaging, the CDN and the buffer on your screen, so the notification lands first. The phone already knows the score the television has not shown.
I have worked behind the scenes in this industry long enough to feel a small, stupid smugness when it happens. Not a good look for a grown man. I own it. The real cost lands on everyone who does not know why, feels the spoiler, and blames the stream.
The sharp edge of sync is that notification, and it is the cheapest thing to fix, because it is addressed to a single device.
The encouraging part is that some of the biggest names are already moving. The BBC is closing the iPlayer gap. Sky built Real Time. Amazon says its delivery stays synchronized across your devices. MLB holds its alerts back by thirty seconds. Tennis TV, YouTube TV and ESPN ship real spoiler controls.
Dolby OptiView is focus heavily on stream syncronization.
I pulled the full rundown together for paying members. Who has shipped what, how far along they are, and which moves you can borrow if you run a platform. Link in the comments.
If you run a sports platform, give every fan a delayed-alert option today, then go and sync the stream. Whoever lands the notification on the goal instead of ahead of it wins a second every fan will feel.
