10 Things To Consider: Sky Buys ITV. The UK Broadcast Map Just Got Redrawn.
How I read it? There is such a level of agitation in the global media industry that it's either a signal of high energy and opportunity (I doubt it) or a delayed check with reality coming home.

📺 The biggest shake-up in British commercial television in a generation.
I read it on LinkedIn before it hit the wires, straight from Sky CEO Dana Strong's post. Fitting, given where we all live now.
Here is the shape of it. Comcast bought a streaming platform, an advertising business and the reach to run both. ITV Studios walks away as a standalone company, which sets up the next deal before this one closes. Regulators hold the timeline, and news plurality is the pressure point.

10 Things To Consider 👇
1️⃣ 💷 The money. £1.2bn cash at completion, up to £200m more in 2028 if ITV advertising tops £1.7bn in FY2027. The top line rides on next year's ad market.
2️⃣ 🎬 ITV Studios walks free. Standalone, cash-generative, and a takeover target the day this closes. Watch this one.
3️⃣ 📡 Comcast bought the platform. ITVX, the ad inventory and the data, wired into the Sky and Peacock stack.
4️⃣ 📊 Advertising is the whole game. Analysts put a combined Sky and ITV above 70% of UK TV advertising. The companies point to 10% of digital ad spend. The regulator has to decide which market it is measuring.
5️⃣ 📰 ITN is the hardest knot. Sky ends up an indirect 20% shareholder in the newsroom that feeds ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5.
6️⃣ ⚖️ The regulators have real work to do. CMA, Ofcom, and a possible public interest review on plurality. Longstop date 6 July 2028.
7️⃣ 🔒 The content lock-in. A £2.1bn supply deal to 2032 keeps Coronation Street, Emmerdale, Love Island and I'm a Celebrity free-to-air.
8️⃣ 🌍 One move in a bigger wave. Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, Banijay and All3Media. Legacy media scaling up against Netflix and YouTube.
9️⃣ 🏢 The NBCUniversal endgame. Sky and ITV M&E fold into NBCUniversal once Comcast completes its planned separation.
🔟 👥 The people questions land first. Who runs content, whether two newsrooms survive, who moves to Osterley. The share price barely moved, up about 1% to 83p, because the market priced this in months ago.

📩 There is a lot more under the hood. Paid members on my Substack get the full breakdown:
📄 The annotated deal, every number from the official filing in plain English
🗓️ A regulatory tracker from the signed agreement to the 2028 longstop
🧩 A vendor briefing on where the openings sit for the next 18 months
🗺️ A map of the whole consolidation wave

"Probably because Ghana never colonised Europe"
A history lesson hiding inside the World Cup team sheets.

I keep hearing the same thing at this World Cup, in comment threads and on live broadcasts. A squad comes on screen and someone starts counting faces, deciding out loud who looks like they belong in the shirt. The tone runs from lazy to openly racist.

The sharpest reply I have seen to all of it came from one exchange online.

❌ Tweet: Not a single white player in the Ghana team.
✅ Reply: Probably because Ghana never colonised Europe.

I work with data, so I wanted to check it properly. I took all 48 nations at the FIFA World Cup 2026 and marked which had been a colony or a protectorate, who ran them, and the year they reached independence or sovereignty.

The full table, all 48 nations with their rulers and independence dates, plus a note on why turning this much history into a grid felt uncomfortable, is in the piece.

To be clear, I have no opinion on where players should choose to play, which passport they carry, or how a nation grows its football (asking for a friend). I did not check anyone's origin. This maps countries and their history, and individual players stay out of it.

posts.text:
Last week I was on the BBC Radio for the first time.
The programme was The Inquiry, presented by Tanya Beckett, and the question was a big one. Is technology ruining sport?
My answer is no. Technology is rewriting the contract. It makes the calls more accurate and it takes some of the argument out of the game, and both of those are true at the same time.
They opened the episode with me on the Lampard ghost goal. Bloemfontein, 2010, England against Germany, a ball a clear foot over the line that nobody gave. That miss is the reason goal line technology and VAR exist today. I walked through how VAR actually works, because plenty of fans still think the machine overrules the referee. It does not. The room advises. The referee decides.
Then three voices I have been thinking about since. Otto Koblinger on why Hawk-Eye is never perfect. Odilon Roble on sport as one of the last safe places we are allowed to disagree. Matt Moore on the pressure of measuring a player on every single serve.
My father shot football for La Stampa for thirty years, back when one photograph was sometimes the only proof a ball had crossed the line. I grew up around those negatives. So I do not treat this technology as something that fell from the sky. The game ran on the eye and the argument for a century before any of it arrived.
Here is the position I left them with. Get the call right and keep the game worth watching. That is the whole brief. The sports that hold both halves will be fine. The ones that win every review and lose the room will not.
Evie Yabsley Amelia Cox

⚽ ❌ ✅ 👀 Proposal: A VAR decisions section on every fifa.com match page
My proposal is simple.
FIFA should add a dedicated VAR decisions section to every match page on fifa.com. One section per fixture, published after the final whistle, every critical call explained in plain language, including the incidents the video team checked and left alone. 📄
England 0-0 Ghana gave us the case study. Ezri Konsa went through Prince Kwabena Adu in the box. No penalty, no on-field review, no explanation. Carlos Queiroz said VAR had gone for a coffee. ☕
Here is the catch. FIFA's visible transparency mostly speaks when the process turns formal. The most argued-about moment of the match was the one it skips: the silent check. 🔇

😎 Full disclosure. I am not a referee, and I have no decisive opinion on the Konsa call, because I do not know every rule in play. That is why I want this. I want to see the reasoning. I have spent close to forty years in broadcast, data and streaming, so it comes from somewhere even if I turn out to be wrong.

Here is the case:
1️⃣ The non-call is the gap. The silent check produces no announcement and no explanation. A match page closes exactly that hole.
2️⃣ One official home. Under the fixture on fifa.com, signed by the refereeing department. No leaks, no selective briefings, no guesswork.
3️⃣ Plain language. Incident, minute, law, the on-field call, whether VAR checked it and why. Thirty seconds to read.
4️⃣ It protects officials. A reasoned public record shows the work. The vacuum is what feeds the pile-on.
5️⃣ The pieces already exist. The Premier League runs Match Officials: Mic'd Up and clarified more than 325 incidents through its Match Centre account. IFAB already lets competitions have the referee explain decisions publicly.
6️⃣ Boring, fast, mobile, multilingual. Posted the morning after, the same template every match.
The argument about referees is permanent. Feed it accurate material and it gets better, and shorter. 🔁

FIFA has opened the process up this World Cup, with mics on referees and decisions on the big screens. The last step is one page.
Build it. 🏗️

Would you read it after every match? 👇

Retention Zone Ep. 82 — Yannick Ramcke (GM OTT, OneFootball)

⚽ OneFootball and the Closing Monetisation Gap
Two years after his first Retention Zone visit, Yannick Manuel Ramcke is back. We checked what held up and what shifted in the subscription business, and the answers got sharp.

Here is what stuck with me 👇
🎯 Churn is still the holy grail. The mood moved from acquisition at all costs to retention and bottom line, because OTT adoption is saturated and growth has plateaued.
💸 Two levers, two logics. Acquisition is a matter of spending money. Retention is a matter of pricing, because a subscription is a value exchange the fan reassesses every month. "You need to prove yourself every single month."
🤖 AI sits across the whole stack. Data was never the bottleneck. What changed is everything downstream: shorter feedback loops, faster iteration, personalisation that scales down to cohorts and individuals.
🏗️ One platform, three models. The white label build lets clubs and rights owners run D2C on OneFootball, pulling the platform across AVOD, TVOD and SVOD at once.
📺 The freshest insight: club TV channels at €1.99 to €2.99 show surprising retention. Price it low enough and cancelling costs more effort than staying. "The shown consideration is not even a consideration anymore."
💡 His bet for the industry: "Where there is engagement, there's willingness to pay." For some segments, short form itself could become a paid product, as long as it stays live.

posts.text:
🗽🏀 ⚽ Can you imagine New York being cheerful?

ALERT: Personal and a bit humourous, emotional, piece.

I was half-listening to Seth Meyers the other night when he said New York is in a party mood right now.
My first thought: wait. New York City?
You can say many true things about that city. Cheerful has never been one of them. It is spiky. It is fast. It is a little annoyed with you for walking too slow.
This week it went and got happy anyway.
The Knicks won the title in five, their first since 1973. Fifty-three years of waiting, paid back in a single night. The World Cup is in town. ⚽

Nobody waited longer than Spike Lee, courtside through every miserable spring.
Years ago, before you could order anything online, I used to buy his screenplays at a Barnes & Noble in Manhattan. Last November he came to Turin, my city, to collect a lifetime award at the Torino Film Festival, and I got to put a question to him at the press conference. The New York man in my town, after all the years I spent buying his New York stories.
I support Torino. Granata. Our last Scudetto was 1976. I know what a long wait feels like, so I am the last person who will tell a happy crowd to calm down.
Here is the thought that snuck up on me.

I work in sports media and tech. On a normal Tuesday it can feel like a silly way to spend a life. Doctors keep people alive. Scientists move us forward. I help keep a stream steady when a shot ends a 53-year drought.
Then a night like this lands and the whole equation flips. What we build lets millions of people sit inside the same feeling at the same second.

In Atlanta, a 40-year-old goalkeeper from Cape Verde named Vozinha held Spain to 0-0 in his country's first ever World Cup. Seven saves. He wept at the final whistle. His mother could not get a US visa in time to be there. Joy and a closed door, in the same shot.
Back in 2008, working the Olympics, the people at NBC told me a thing I never managed to put down.

Sport is all about a flag, a hero, and a story.

Still true. This week had all three.
I did not have any of it on my list for 2026. I am very glad to be wrong.

posts.text:
🏈 📺 10 Things To Consider About Fox and Roku
Fox just paid $22 billion for the home screen.

The Fox Corporation and Roku deal is a move to own the front door to 100 million living rooms. Roku in 2026 is a connected-TV advertising business sitting on an operating system. The hardware is the smallest part of the story. Fox bought the layer that decides what a household sees first when the TV wakes up.

Here are 10 Things To Consider 👇

1️⃣ The home screen is the real asset. Device sales are under 10% of Roku revenue.
2️⃣ The engine is CTV advertising. Roku ad revenue hit $613M last quarter, up 27%.
3️⃣ Free ad-supported TV is now Fox's main bet. Tubi and The Roku Channel under one roof.
4️⃣ Subscription stays in play. Fox now owns the in-app purchase rails on Roku devices.
5️⃣ Live sport is the anchor. NFL, MLB, the World Cup and Fox News pull the whole household in.
6️⃣ Neutrality is the big question. A content owner now runs an open platform.
7️⃣ The hardware is a drag. Low-margin manufacturing inside a content and advertising business.
8️⃣ Aggregation is the thesis. Whoever owns the front door owns discovery.
9️⃣ The market is unconvinced. Fox stock fell as much as 18% on the news.
🔟 The signal travels. Every broadcaster now has to ask who owns their front door.

📌 The full piece goes deeper: the deal in detail, why the market flinched, and the European read, where Roku is far smaller and the home screen belongs to Samsung, Amazon and LG.

🔒 For paid subscribers: five questions worth asking, and what the deal means for every vendor in our industry, from CTV ad-tech and measurement to FAST infrastructure, billing and sports-rights holders.

Last night I wanted to research the DAZN interactive element while watching FIFA World Cup 2026™ - Canada, Mexico and the United States match Brasil - Morocco, on my laptop, but had to stop after few minutes for the incredibly disturbing racist and fascist messages that the chat contained - especially against Morocco.
Also, I was watching with my son Miles 11yrs old and others.

This is not just yet another case of "we should not have fans chat", I have been involved for too long to simplify my solution to that.
 Two aspects.
1. The sadly obvious acknowledgement of how these occasion highlights the worst parts of the worst people (especially if the can hide their identity, but not exclusively). Also considering there maybe legal consequences.
2. The fact that even in the age of AI these things are still happening, makes me doubt we really need fans chat - even if for years I hoped they could add value. We are back in 1999…

I am curious to see if DAZN makes some changes going forward.
My suggestion apart from removing the chat all together.
1. Are we sure DAZN is using the most advanced tool to clean the chat in real time? (no idea)
2. Can DAZN add a selection UI to just get interactive elements and other controlled experiences (maybe it was there, did not see it, I will check again tonight). We would have loved to engage with those the whole game...
3. I don't want to only talk about the platform here... What is with these people! Personal responsibility should not be diluted by troubled digital interface
4. I wanted to see if I could report users but the speed of the flow was so high that it was impossible to do that
5. DAZN has a page dedicated to this - link in the comments - with an explanation of their methodology this statement: "Our commitment
At DAZN, we are dedicated to maintaining a vibrant, safe, and inclusive environment for all sports fans. Your support and collaboration are key to making it happen."

So no analysis from me today on the FIFA World Cup fan digital engagement.

Images below:
1. How we watched on the kitchen table of my country home
2. Composition (no AI my manual terrible image stitching) of what we did not want to watch
I have some images with the hateful comments which I am not sharing to avoid promoting their intent.

and by the way - great match!

Deep diving the Drake Star quarterly report has become quite a habit for me. This quarter the headline says $130.6 billion across 239 deals. One transaction, Paramount Skydance buying Warner Bros. Discovery, accounts for $110 billion of it. The real story starts after you set it aside, and the report itself half admits it, footnoting WBD out of its own charts.

The 10 things:
1️⃣ Read the headline number twice: 107 deals describe the market, the $130B does the marketing
2️⃣ Sports data companies want to be media companies (Genius Sports + Legend, $1.2B)
3️⃣ Youth sports is now a private equity platform thesis (LiveBarn, $400M)
4️⃣ The B2B team operations layer is consolidating fast (Teamworks + PFF + Sportlogiq)
5️⃣ Prediction markets crossed the institutional line (Kalshi at $22B, ICE into Polymarket, and days ago Sportradar + Kalshi)
6️⃣ Wearables outgrew the locker room, and the cycle is back in its up phase (WHOOP at $10.1B)
7️⃣ Creator-led formats are capitalized competitors (Kings League, $63M)
8️⃣ 80% of financings were early-stage: the 2028-2030 M&A inventory is being seeded right now
9️⃣ Over $4B in new funds is aimed at the vendor layer (Otro, Bruin, Athvance)
🔟 Public markets reward scale: decide if you are the platform or the add-on

⚽ 10 Things To Consider: Sports Tech and Media at the FIFA World Cup 2026™ - Canada, Mexico and the United States
🎙️ I recorded an interview with BBC World Service on officiating technology, still to air. Prepping for it pulled me deep into the VAR and offside machinery, so I widened the lens.
The 2026 World Cup puts the whole sports media stack on one table. Officiating, rights, streaming, platforms, AI. Most of it has appeared before. This time every piece has been enhanced, and several are new.

Here are the 10 things I am watching as the football starts. 👇
1️⃣ ⚽ The offside system now alerts the assistant referee directly. Faster calls, fewer long stoppages.
2️⃣ 🧍 Every one of the 1,248 players is 3D scanned into a digital twin, used for offside decisions and broadcast replays.
3️⃣ 🔧 Officiating is really four suppliers. Hawk-Eye, Lenovo, Adidas with KINEXON, and Hisense.
4️⃣ 🎥 Referees wear body cameras, and some markets get audio of their decisions. The biggest trust upgrade in the package.
5️⃣ 💰 Fox is paying under $500m for US rights valued at $1bn to $1.5bn, on a deal locked in back in 2014.
6️⃣ 📺 US streaming is fragmented by design. Fox, FS1, Fox One, Tubi, Telemundo, Peacock.
7️⃣ 📱 YouTube and TikTok are a promotional layer. The first ten minutes and highlights flow through the broadcasters' own channels.
8️⃣ 🎬 FIFA+ launched exclusively on DAZN on 4 June, five days before kickoff.
9️⃣ 🤖 Football AI Pro gives all 48 teams the same analytics baseline.
🔟 🌍 None of this exists below the elite. The gap to grassroots football widens every cycle.

👉 For my Substack Subscribers (paid) I went deeper on the officiating tech on its own. The full breakdown of VAR, semi-automated offside, the connected ball, referee comms and what is new for 2026 is in a separate deep dive.

🎯 One-Hit Wonders: what happens when a single club video swallows a whole season.
One Osasuna short pulled 38.2 million views.
That clip alone is 48% of everything Osasuna has ever uploaded to YouTube. In their entire YouTube lifetime.

I built a feature inside YouTube Football Tracker (YTFT) that ranks club videos by how far they sit above their channel's own season average.

📐 The math:
Lift = video views ÷ channel's average views per video this season

I ran it across the top five European leagues. The top ten this season:

⚽ 1. C.A. Osasuna (LaLiga) · Víctor Muñoz golazo · Lift 8,980
⚽ 2. Real Sociedad (LaLiga) · the Saturday derby win · Lift 7,233
⚽ 3. Real Sociedad (LaLiga) · Take Kubo's first goal · Lift 7,182
⚽ 4. RCD Espanyol de Barcelona (LaLiga) · "We love our academy" · Lift 7,068
⚽ 5. RCD Espanyol de Barcelona (LaLiga) · "The Minion's journey" · Lift 5,264
⚽ 6. Real Sociedad (LaLiga) · "bocata de otra galaxia" · Lift 4,741
⚽ 7. RCD Espanyol de Barcelona (LaLiga) · dogs adoption walk-out · Lift 3,642
⚽ 8. Deportivo Alavés (LaLiga) · "Work, work, work" · Lift 2,471
⚽ 9. RCD Mallorca (LaLiga) · "MATEEEOOOO" · Lift 2,212
⚽ 10. Sunderland AFC (Premier League) · "DAN BALLARD" · Lift 2,125

The big clubs are absent from this list and the math is the reason. Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern, PSG produce viral content as a baseline. Their season average is already pulled high. When everything is big, nothing stands far above the line.

🎮 He also plays EA SPORTS FC 26 on his PlayStation, and he has no phone of his own. FIFA's new flagship is mobile-first and built around Netflix. The console in his room already belongs to EA.
📅 That is the whole story in one room. On 28 May FIFA announced an updated Digital Football Strategy with Roblox, Konami, Netflix, SEGA, Gamefam, Mythical, Epic and Solace on board. The World Cup opens on 11 June. Fourteen days.
🧠 The strategy is sound. A multi-partner ecosystem is the right answer to losing EA, and the FIFAe esports layer already works at scale. The timing and the distribution are where it slips.

📝 I wrote it up as 10 Things To Consider, leading on the go-to-market and what the move says about the FIFA brand without the game that made it famous. Full read 👉 below

🔒 For paid Substack subscribers I added the practitioner's cut: an 8-point launch checklist any rights holder or vendor can run before a multi-partner play, the 6 signals I am tracking through the World Cup window, and a follow-up where I grade FIFA against the checklist once the game lands.

posts.text:
💰 The $500 Million Bargain

📊 Fox is paying less than $500 million to broadcast the 2026 World Cup. Industry analysts put the real market value at between $1 billion and $1.5 billion.

🏟️ Tariq Panja in the The New York Times this weekend filled in how that happened. A soundproof room below FIFA's Zurich headquarters in March 2014. A decision made under pressure to avoid a Fox lawsuit over the Qatar date change. An extension granted eleven years before the tournament, at a price set against a 2014 view of the world.

🎞️ I have been around long enough to remember when media rights cycles ran three and four editions deep as standard. Most of my working life has been shaped by those cycles, by what they paid for, by what they assumed about the next decade. The Fox-FIFA case is the most visible example of a pattern that runs through sports rights every time the calendar gets tight. Federations trade competition for certainty under pressure, and discover years later what certainty actually cost.

🎯 The wider point sits above the news. Federations now know long deals carry real downside. The question is whether their growth models are good enough to price what they are signing. Fox-FIFA was a failure of forecasting under pressure. The federations signing the next round of long deals are betting their forecasting has improved. Some of those bets will be right. The ones that are wrong will look like Fox-FIFA in 2036.

📬 I wrote it up on A Guy With A Scarf. Free article on the deal and the lesson, with a paid appendix for subscribers that goes deeper. The appendix covers the full arc of FIFA's US English-language rights from 1994 to 2030, five long-dated rights bets that aged worst and five that aged best across thirty years of sports media, the Telemundo and Canadian extensions no one is talking about, the Burzaco testimony layer with the legal context, a working framework of seven questions to ask before signing past one cycle, and what all of this means for the 2030 World Cup auction.

🎙️ Retention Zone Ep. 81 Part 2 is out.

Gilles Domartini, CEO of Cleeng, on Agents in Production and the Death of the Dashboard (Part 2 of 2)

Four agents in production, the guardrails behind them, and a revised forecast on when the dashboard finally dies.

Part one covered what Gilles saw across his US tour: a frozen enterprise, a booming creator economy, a transfer of value out of legacy SaaS into AI infrastructure. The product answer in one line: ship working systems inside the workflows clients already use, and build the guardrails before the agents.

🤖 At NAB Cleeng announced agents in production, framed against AI slop and slideware. Partners and clients want proof at scale.

🎯 The onboarding agent acts as a coach across every step on the platform, paired with the freemium tier that lets new customers start Cleeng for free up to 10,000 subscribers.

📊 The analyst agent is the one most used by existing clients. A typical deployment carries around 60 dashboards covering MRR, ARPU, LTV, upgrades, downgrades, campaign management across web, Roku, app stores. Two hours of Monday morning digging becomes a single prompt: "Roku had an issue. Your debit cards are converting at a lower rate. Win-back campaign twenty-two performed well, this one didn't, we recommend you do this."

⚙️ The offer setup agent takes the recommendation and creates the campaign inside the platform. The analyst spots the opportunity. The offer agent ships it.

🔒 The hard part isn't the AI. The guardrails consumed the time. Client data segregation, PII removal, role-based access at the prompt level. Finance sees financial data. Customer care sees user interactions and churn risk. Selling an agent into a media business means selling a security model, a permissions architecture and an audit trail.

💬 UX as quality of interaction. Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT moved the bar. Cleeng is working toward an experience that feels like a subscriber retention coach sitting next to you.

📅 The September 27 prediction. At IBC 2024 Gilles predicted dashboards would be gone within two years. He revised the call: "We will still have a dashboard in September 2026. But in September 2027, I'm definitely not sure." Cleeng is moving fast on headless. Partners create an offer or pull analytics from inside Slack, copilot, MediaKind, Accedo, Univision or ATP.

🎯 The bet. The winners over the next 24 months are the vendors who ship working systems inside their clients' existing workflows, with the permissions architecture to make those systems trustworthy, and who move faster than the consolidation around them. The dashboard era ends on a date Gilles will not yet name. The work to be useful after that date starts now.

posts.text:
⚽ 🟥 50 years ago today. The day I put the Toro anthem on the balcony for the whole neighbourhood to hear

16 May 1976. I was eleven. When the news came from Perugia that Juventus had lost and Torino were champions of Italy, I did the most sacred thing I could think of: I put the stereo on the balcony of our flat in Turin, turned the volume to the maximum, and played the Toro anthem.
I still have the granata flag from that day. No shield sewn on. There had not been time yet.
My father Piero De Marchis was at the Stadio Comunale that Sunday as a staff photographer for La Stampa. There is a photograph that catches him at pitch-side just behind Graziani while the celebration grows around them. Fifty years on, I have written a long piece about that afternoon. Here are the layers:

⚽ The team. A working-class side built at the Filadelfia, modernised by Gigi Radice's full-pitch pressing, captained by Claudio Sala. Pulici top scorer with 21 goals, Graziani 15. Final table Torino 45, Juventus 43.

🏘️ The city. From my balcony I could see la casa del Toro thirty metres away: a ten-storey block in Vanchiglietta where Claudio Sala and other players lived. In 1973–74 I used to go roller-skating with the daughter of then-coach Gustavo Giagnoni. I watched Aldo Agroppi play football with his son in the garden in front of the building. They were idols already, and the distance was smaller.

⛰️ The hill. Twenty-seven years and twelve days after Superga, the title came back. Gian Paolo Ormezzano, then editor of Tuttosport, wrote the headline that still defines the club: "Lassù qualcuno ti ama". Up there, someone loves you.

📺 The docuseries. From Friday on Sky Sport, a three-part series with the very same title. Sky Creative Agency used generative AI to bring historical photographs to life from the protagonists' accounts. A cultivated, legitimate use of the technology, where AI fills the holes in visual memory. The memory of the Toro has always been made of holes, of lost home movies, of grainy photographs. Those machines now give back what time had taken.
Being Toro is a grammar. A syntax of melancholy, of waiting, of loyalty to an idea of football that is also an idea of the world. You support Toro for the pleasure of never choosing the easy road.

I wrote this one for me, for my father, for the boys still up there at Superga, and for anyone who has ever put a stereo on a balcony for a reason that only a city can understand.

🎙️ Retention Zone Ep. 81 is out in two parts
Gilles Domartini, CEO of Cleeng, on the Frozen Enterprise and the Transfer of Value (Part 1 of 2)

A frozen enterprise, a booming creator economy, and the rotation of capital out of legacy SaaS.

The most useful number from my conversation with Gilles is 24. That is the horizon beyond which large investors and enterprise buyers in media tech currently cannot see. For the first time in 20 years of tech, the next two years are harder to predict than the past 20.

📍 Two months in the US, both coasts, NAB Las Vegas and the Devoncroft executive summit. Gilles came back with a clear read.

📉 Investment in media and entertainment tech declining 2 to 4% on average every year. The slowdown is constant.

🚀 One category is booming. The creator economy keeps growing on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok against Warner Bros. and Paramount. SMB creators are the fast-growing middle where margins remain less compressed.

🥶 Why enterprises are frozen. Large investors deploy on four to six-year horizons. They cannot model that today. Paramount-Skydance, Netflix and Warner Bros., Harmonic-MediaKind. Deltatre going through organisational changes too. CFOs demanding savings. AI sitting on top as a productivity question with change management attached. The result is a frozen state in parts of the enterprise category.

💸 Where the money went. Atlassian, Salesforce, Snowflake, GitLab dropped fifty percent in three months. That money was reallocated to Anthropic, Google, NVIDIA. Twelve Labs and Eleven Labs landing big funding.

⏱️ The 24-month window is short. The required moves are not subtle. Waiting carries a specific price: missing the window and reading about the consolidation that followed in someone else's deck.

🔜 In part two: the four agents Cleeng put into production at NAB, the guardrails behind them, and Gilles's revised prediction on when the dashboard finally dies.

🎯 Do You Have Agency?

It is the buzzword of the moment. Every CEO talking about hiring, every VC explaining who made it, every leadership consultant who used to say "ownership." I heard it enough times that I went to document myself, because the surface meaning was hiding something more specific.

Here is what I found, and why it matters now.

🤖 AI is what makes agency valuable
When execution gets cheap, deciding what to execute is the only premium left. Two teams with the same AI stack will diverge based on who points the tools at the right problems. AI is excellent at doing. It is still terrible at choosing.

⚡ Agency is acting when acting is the right move
People with it see a gap and close it. People without it see a gap and write a memo. Bravery for its own sake is a different thing.

🏟️ Our industry punishes it
Sports and media tech runs on long sales cycles, federation politics, broadcaster relationships, procurement reviews. The structure rewards waiting. In decades inside this industry, the pattern is consistent: the good outcomes come from someone deciding to do something that was not in the brief. The vendors that grow figured out how to move at the speed of the audience while the rest of the industry moves at the speed of the procurement department.

💼 The PE signal
Private equity buyers do not wait. The playbook is mixed in outcomes, sometimes real value, sometimes hollowed-out EBITDA gains. What is consistent is the speed differential, and that tells you how much agency the previous ownership was leaving on the table.

🔑 The takeaway
The opposite of agency is permission. Stop asking for it.

📋 For paid subscribers
The Do You Have Agency? Checklist. Thirty questions across three roles in sports and media tech: leadership, vendor, and client. Designed to make you flinch. If none of them do, the test is broken. Or you are.

📺 📲 10 Things To Consider After the 2026 NAB Streaming Summit
Two years ago I was on stage at the Streaming Summit in Vegas. This year I was not. So I did what we do when we miss the room. I read everything.

Very thankful that Dan Rayburn publishes every session in full, with video. I pulled the transcripts and reverse engineered the conference over a weekend.

🔟 10 Things To Consider
🤖 1. AI moved from the roadmap to the rundown. The PGA TOUR session with Phil Green and Eric Hanson put the number on it: 7,000 AI highlight clips a week. That is a working production line.
🏟️ 2. Live sports is still the hardest problem in streaming. The Engineering the Live Sports Pipeline panel said it plainly. Live is the R&D lab. Everyone else is the customer. Yannick Manuel Ramcke from OneFootball reminded the room that even with every telemetry pipeline lit, eyes on the glass still matters.
📺 3. Pay TV still owns 85% of US live sports viewing. Dan Rayburn opened day two with that humility check. Build sports streaming products with that number in mind.
🧩 4. The distribution math is in flux. FAST, AVOD, SVOD, carrier-OTT all coexist. The Bundling and Distribution panel with Mike Callahan, Brian Dunlap, Chris Buckley and Steven "Claw" Jalicy made it clear: there is no template.
🎯 5. Personalization is moving from a row on the home screen to the live moment. Patrick Carroll at NASCAR and Paul Boustead at Dolby OptiView are building personalization that lives inside the experience itself.
🔍 6. Discovery is still broken, and chatbots are not the rescue. Bernd Riefler's study across ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini made that clear. The metadata work matters more than the chatbot.
⚡ 7. Ultra-low latency at premium bitrate is now table stakes. Derik Yarnell at Comcast walked through the 30 Mbps RealTime4K stream of Super Bowl LX with Dolby Vision and Atmos.
🧠 8. The frame-based streaming model may be on its way out. Sandeep Tiku at DAZN argued for transmitting change and reconstructing the experience on the device. Take it seriously.
🎬 9. Content libraries are becoming searchable scene by scene. John Sculley at VideoMagic and Keir Shepherd at Encompass made the case. Library is now a verb. You query it.
🔗 10. The stack is the product. The PGA TOUR runs a 165,000 sq ft facility weaving multiple vendors. Whoever owns the integration owns the experience.

Read the article. Then book the flight for 2027.

🏃‍➡️ SportsPro London 2026, Day Two: The Reality Check Sharpened
Day two went deeper into the media track. Same signal as day one, different instruments.

🤖 Paola Marinone (BuzzMyVideos) joined me on camera at the Oval. Her opening line set the tone. Asking yourself the right questions is what produces the right answers. Intellectual honesty is the prerequisite for new business models, new ideas, new value. The silver bullet is the part that does not exist. Her bridge to Bengu Atamer's YouTube-as-TV thesis was clean. New assets, new sponsorship packages, new revenue lines on the P&L. This is business.
🤖 Chris Stone (SportsPro) opened the media track with a twelve-month scan. Big tech is in sports rights for real. YouTube streamed an NFL game. @Apple holds F1 in the US. Netflix has NFL Christmas Day. ESPN launched D2C. In Europe, the BBC and YouTube partnership with fifty bespoke channels is the watershed. The Bundesliga UK approach across Sky Sports, Amazon, BBC iPlayer, YouTube and Mark Goldbridge's channel is the case study to watch. Casimiro will broadcast all 104 games of the 2026 World Cup. Chris's painful number: ninety-six of the top one hundred US TV shows in 2025 were sports. The UK top ten is Traitors and I'm a Celebrity. Top five sports take eighty percent of all media rights revenue.
🤖 David Gibbs (WBD Sports Europe) with Greg Burns (Reuters Imagen) walked through the @HBO Max consolidation. 130M subscribers, 35,000 live events this year. Milano Cortina pulled 3X the viewing subscribers of Beijing 2022. His answer to Nick Meacham's live versus non-live question: none of the non-live stuff exists if the live product is not as good as it can be. His closer: you come for Liverpool and you stay for Dragons.
🤖 Patrick Mostboeck (Sportradar) took the AI session into product. Generative AI gives new tools, it does not collapse the work. Headline deployment: NBA Peacock Performance View on Peacock. One in four NBA users opted into the augmented stream. Less is more. Next layer is prediction.
Both David Gibbs and Patrick Mostboeck acknowledged me from the stage. After thirty-five years building and launching streaming services for sport, that recognition lands. Streaming did not become what it is today by accident. Thank you both.
Prove the ROI one use case at a time. Pick the lowest hanging fruit. Let the next use case earn the right to exist. That is the only signal worth carrying out of the Oval.

posts.text:
🎯 10 Things To Consider About DAZN Buying ViewLift

A $100M deal that says more about where the sports OTT vendor market is going than about ViewLift itself.

I sat across from Manik Bambha and the ViewLift team a few years back in a similar process. Prepared in a way rarer than it should be in this industry.

1️⃣ Price tells a story. $100M is small. Bain Capital and Nextalia bought Deltatre in 2022 for around $800M. DAZN is paying for entry, relationships, and speed. Disclosure. I worked at Deltatre for many years before leaving. Everything I write about it comes from public sources only.
2️⃣ Timing is the calendar. Main Street Sports Group is winding down. 20 NBA and NHL teams in the open market before 2026-27.
3️⃣ The product is optionality. Per Sports Business Journal, DAZN is pitching three models. ViewLift Classic, full rights at $8-15M annually, and a streaming hub.
4️⃣ B2B2C and SaaS is the actual strategy. DAZN CEO Shay Segev wants to be infrastructure as well as a destination.
5️⃣ The end-to-end sports OTT vendor model is shifting. NBA's investment arm took an equity stake in MediaKind in September 2025. Three months later MediaKind acquired Harmonic's video business for $145M. The vendor-client boundary is no longer where it used to be.
6️⃣ The market is consolidating. Deltatre acquired Endeavor Streaming in July 2025. Bending Spoons bought Brightcove for $233M and Vimeo for $1.38B. Now DAZN buys ViewLift.
7️⃣ The deal structure tells a story. ViewLift shareholders are rolling under the DAZN umbrella. Equity in a buyer is only attractive if you believe the buyer is going somewhere worth being. DAZN has indicated it will be profitable this year with accelerating growth. (UPDATED)
8️⃣ The competitive set is crowded. Amazon, ESPN, Fubo, Victory+, YouTube TV, Gray Media, Scripps, Nexstar, and Kiswe are all in the same conversations.
9️⃣ The Ted Leonsis fact. ViewLift was founded by Leonsis. The product encodes a worldview that comes from the team side of the business.
🔟 The B2B vendor lesson. Technology expertise alone does not earn a seat at the rights conversation. The pure technology supplier role is being squeezed from above by hyperscalers and from below by content operators.

❓ What I am still unsure about
Whether DAZN can run three models at once. Whether the bet on local-rights fragmentation is correct.
DAZN moved from distant national rights bidder to operational US partner in a single $100M transaction. The people inside ViewLift, including Manik Bambha and the leadership Rick Allen anchors, are the reason this deal has a real chance of delivering in practice as much as on paper.

posts.text:
🤖 SportsPro London 2026: five sessions that made the room sound honest

I moderated a panel on monetising fragmented audiences with Bobby Nightingale (Bath Rugby) and Stefan Lavén (Data Talks).
Bobby opened with the most honest line of the event. Bath runs ticketing, CRM, CDP, email, e-wallets, push, most not talking to each other. Bath has a data identification problem, not a growth one. Stefan argued for the plumbing. Bobby pushed back: plumbing matters once you have a clear value exchange.
Stefan's stat: first ROI comes from reactivating idle fans in the database. Bobby retargeted opted-outs. One signed shirt, one email, 42% back. On AI, Bobby says the value is in workflows.
A plug for Retention Zone. Reactivation is underrated.

Nick Meacham (CEO, SportsPro) opened with eight industry dreams against eight realities. Media rights revenues are hyper-concentrated at the top. Investors are a release valve, not a saviour. Sport is not built for venture capital. Engagement is massive, the bucket is leaky. Fans do not like paying. AI delivers efficiency, not yet top-line growth. He warned us this would be a reality check. He did not hold any punch.

Michael Payne with Samuel Agini (Financial Times) was fifty years of stories nobody had written down. Cortina was far more successful than anyone dared imagine. The TV product is in good shape. The organisation running the show is the issue. On Russia, he expects them back for LA28. Two predictions that stayed with me: within a decade the NFL makes a hostile takeover of World Rugby, and Volleyball World (where Payne now chairs after CVC's investment) has overtaken football as Japan's number two sport.
A call for Olympic athletes' media rights.
Read the book. He is the Michael Wolff of sport business.

Bengu Atamer (BuzzMyVideos) made the case that YouTube has become TV. 1.1 billion watch hours. Fastest-growing segment is over 65. Four-asset framework: always-on, searchable, archive, exclusivity. Each one is a sponsorship product. Her FIFA-YouTube World Cup breakdown was the clearest of the day. Three layers: ten minutes of live rights to creators, archive vault opened up, co-livestreams. F1 is sitting on a double-digit million sponsorship package on YouTube and giving it away free. Her question: how much money are you leaving on the table.

Claudio Demmer (VfL Wolfsburg) presented the most operationally honest AI case study of the day. 91 percent weekly active users. 100 active GPTs. Five service companies replaced. Six-figure productivity gain.
The framing made me uncomfortable. Blind excitement and low empathy. A recipe for disaster.

🤖 The takeaway. The hype cycle is exhausting itself. What is left is harder, slower, more rewarding. Stop pitching the Northern Star. Pick the lowest hanging fruit, prove the ROI, let the next use case earn the right to exist.

posts.text:
📺 📲 YouTube TV's custom multiview, the architecture question, and the pro-YouTube echo chamber around it (an all-things YouTube post)

YouTube TV switched on fully customisable multiview this week. Four live streams, mix and match across packages including NFL Sunday Ticket. The user value is real. Multiple games on Sunday afternoon, RSN paired with a national broadcast, the sports bar pattern reproduced in a single subscription. That is the win.

Dan Rayburn flagged the limitations cleanly within an hour of the announcement: live only, family-friendly exclusions, less than 5% of older devices on a reduced UX, no computer support. The computer exclusion is the most telling. This is a living-room and mobile product.

The architecture question is where this gets interesting. My assumption is server-side compositing, with YouTube doing the work on its own infrastructure and delivering a single unified feed. I may be wrong. YouTube's 2023 launch post stated they "moved the processing requirements to happen on YouTube's servers." Jan Ozer's December 2025 analysis at Streaming Learning Center confirms the architecture and gives the most rigorous breakdown of why it matters. He contrasts YouTube TV's server-side approach with FuboTV's client-side Apple TV implementation that reached only around 13% of their base, and Formula 1 TV's client-side build-your-own with similar availability gaps. Server-side is the only way this scales across older Chromecasts, smart TVs, mobile, and streaming sticks. Client-side multiview is a graveyard.

I have spent years building advanced video experiences and adoption is always the blocker. The capability has usually been there. Working with Dolby OptiView on advanced live experiences, this launch reads as a useful data point on where the compute should live in your stack. YouTube made a deliberate architectural choice. Other operators thinking about advanced video features should ask the same question of their own systems.

Richard Gillis raised a fair question this week about the volume of pro-YouTube content in B2B sports media right now. The launch is real. The architecture is right. The discourse around YouTube is also currently louder than the actual rights distribution map suggests it should be. Holding both at once is the job.
Today at SportsPro London I am meeting BuzzMyVideos. Bengu Atamer's work on the "Event Trap" and the comparison of Roblox and YouTube data on creator-led versus broadcast event approaches is the kind of analysis the industry needs more of. Their YouTube stats work has actually inspired a project I am building in the YouTube analytics space, still in stealth. The questions are better because of this week's launch.

⚙️ 🩷 A love letter to heads of IT

Dear Head of IT,

You were already the person who says no to everything for good reasons. Security, compliance, data protection, vendor sprawl, that one time somebody wanted Dropbox on the corporate network. You usually get blamed for slowing things down and rarely thanked when nothing catches fire.

This month your job changed again.

Blocking does not work anymore. Approval queues do not work anymore. Lovable, Replit Agent, v0, Bolt, Claude Code, Cursor. Every smart non-developer with a weekend and a credit card can now ship a working full-stack app. Internal dashboards, microsites, scrapers, small CRM replacements. And your CEO just sent the 6am email asking why the company is "not using AI enough."

A true story from the early 2000s that explains exactly where we are. I was in a meeting with the president of a large European organisation. He turned to the room and asked why the company should spend several million on a new website when his son had built one in a weekend on WordPress for a thousand euros. The guy was fired a week later for unrelated reasons. The question never was. Twenty years on, swap WordPress for Lovable, swap the son for a product marketer with Claude Code, swap the weekend for an afternoon. That question is now in every executive's head.

My take: stop being the last line of defence. Start being the first line of enablement. Sanction two or three build-your-own-app tools officially with SSO and audit logs. Build a fifteen-minute review conversation, not a six-week approval form. Own the AI and infrastructure budget before every department starts paying for it on personal cards.

The smart people in the company are building whether you bless it or not. Your job is to make sure they build well.

👩‍🎨 A love letter to corporate design leads

Dear Head of Design,
You were already at the mercy of everybody's taste. The CEO has opinions. The CMO has references. The founder's partner once worked in fashion. You manage to ship a coherent system anyway. You deserve a medal. You usually get "can we try it in blue."
This month your job changed (again).

Claude Design went live on April 17. ChatGPT Images 2.0 shipped on April 21. Four days apart. Both sit inside tools your colleagues already pay for. Every single person in your company can now generate a pitch deck, a landing page prototype, a one pager, an infographic, a UI mockup. No Figma license. No design review. A prompt box and some confidence.
The good part is real. Your team can stop spending afternoons on quick internal banners and start spending them on the three decisions per quarter that actually shape the product.
The bad part is the physics problem. When everyone can produce, everyone produces. Monday morning the CEO forwards you a deck generated overnight with a version of your logo nobody has ever seen before, and asks if you can "polish it a bit" before the board meeting at noon.

My take: the design leads who win the next eighteen months are the ones who stop fighting the proliferation and start shaping it. Claim the design system conversation loudly. Define what the tools should not be used for. Move from gatekeeper to editor in chief.
The tools are here. The colleagues are excited. The output is coming whether you bless it or not. Pick up the pen.

🤖 10 things to consider About the Stanford AI Index Report 2026

Part of my Untangling AI series.
Stanford University HAI released the ninth edition of the AI Index. 423 pages. The most comprehensive piece of independent measurement we have on the field.

🚀 1. AI capability is accelerating. The plateau argument is finished. SWE-bench Verified went from 60% to nearly 100% in a single year.
🌏 2. The U.S. and China are running neck and neck. The best U.S. model leads by 2.7% as of March 2026.
✈️ 3. The US talent pipeline is collapsing. Researchers moving to the US dropped 89% since 2017, 80% in the last year alone. AI skills are growing fastest in the UAE, Chile, and South Africa.
🧩 4. The jagged frontier is the most useful concept in the report. Maths olympiad gold, yet 50.1% on reading analog clocks. Robots succeed at 12% of household tasks.
⚡ 5. Adoption hit 53% population-level in three years. Faster than the PC or the internet. Organisational adoption at 88%.
🤖 6. Agent deployment is still in the single digits. The noise is enormous. The installed base is tiny.
📉 7. Productivity gains are real and already moving the labour market for the young. US developers aged 22 to 25 dropped nearly 20% from 2024.
🛡️ 8. Safety measurement is visibly failing. AI incidents rose from 233 to 362. Independent evaluation belongs in the contract.
🏛️ 9. AI sovereignty is the new organising principle of national policy. You are building for a policy map that fragments every quarter.
🤝 10. Experts and the public are 50 points apart on AI's impact on jobs. A technology in motion.

My position after reading all 423 pages: stop waiting for the dust to settle. It will not. The companies that win the next five years are the ones making bets now, with imperfect information, while keeping a short diary of what they got wrong so they can correct quickly.

🔟 📲 10 things to consider on the DAZN Playmakers Programme

When this landed on April 1st, 😎 I checked the date twice. A global creator programme from DAZN? Sounded like a prank. But the more I read, the more it connected to everything DAZN has been building over the past year. So I dug in.

Here are my 😎 10 things to consider:

1️⃣ This already happened once, and it worked. The Club World Cup creator programme last summer reached 2.7 billion viewers. 80% engaged with non-live content. Playmakers makes it permanent.

2️⃣ The CMO is an e-commerce guy. Adam Knappy spent 14 years at THG. His career is conversion funnels and customer acquisition. That tells you how this programme will be measured.

3️⃣ DAZN already owns a creator company. Team Whistle, acquired in 2023, gives Playmakers an in-house production and distribution engine. Real advantage.

4️⃣ The timing is deliberate. FIFA World Cup this summer. FIFA+ relaunching on DAZN. Bundesliga, Serie A, Champions League rights across markets. The content canvas is massive.

5️⃣ The creator value proposition is vague. Platform access and affiliate links are table stakes. Merch and event access are nice. They don't pay rent. The "and more" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

6️⃣ The real test is editorial freedom. 83% trust stat is industry boilerplate. Sports fans smell managed content immediately. If creators feel corporate, they lose credibility fast.

7️⃣ The Bundesliga model is the real benchmark. Live Friday-night match rights to YouTube creators. CazéTV holding FIFA World Cup rights in Brazil. Those are rights deals. Playmakers is social content and event access. Different category.

8️⃣ "Every sport" is probably too ambitious at launch. Football creators are abundant. Other sports have thin pools. The Club World Cup programme worked because it was focused. One sport. One event. One moment.

9️⃣ The playbook looks familiar. If you watch camera or music gear content on YouTube, you've seen this model. Sony drops a new body, every channel has a video up within days. AKAI launches the MPC Sample, same wave. Coordinated seeding that looks organic. DAZN may be building the sports version of this.

🔟 Count the layers DAZN is stacking. Live rights. Whistle. DAZN+. FIFA+. FanZone. Matchroom through 2031. And now Playmakers. That is a lot of moving parts. Creators go where the brand channel cannot. The question is whether the org chart can deliver all of this at the same time.

Retention Zone Ep. 80: Pier Luigi Spagna (WBD) – Retention as an Engine for Profitable Growth
How Warner Bros. Discovery Thinks About Churn, Sport, and Scale

My guest is Pier Luigi Spagna, Vice President of EMEA Retention & Engagement at Warner Bros. Discovery. A fellow Italian with nearly 20 years in DTC marketing across betting, food delivery, startups, and streaming. I found him deeply invested in the craft of retention. The kind of person who has seen enough industries to know what actually works and what is just noise.

And yes we do gesticulate a bit and have quite some energy. That's why you want Italians in your key positions 😎 🇮🇹

A few things that stayed with me from this conversation:
⚙️ Retention is an engine for profitable growth. Pull the acquisition blanket too far on one side and retention suffers. Pull it the other way and you are not growing fast enough. The balance is the job.
📊 At WBD, churn is a company-wide KPI. When the CEO calls it out, everyone aligns. Pier Luigi's team owns that number. They recently moved from marketing into the product growth organization, which gives them direct influence on what subscribers see inside the platform.
⚽ Sport is a fascinating retention challenge. Expensive to acquire, hard to make profitable, easy to churn from. The trick is dual viewership: getting sport subscribers hooked on entertainment content while they are watching their event. The retention rate after a major sport event on HBO Max is significantly higher than it was on Discovery Plus, which was already higher than Eurosport. Content scheduling is a retention lever.
🤖 AI helps with scale and optimization. The strategy still comes from humans. "I don't think it's gonna entirely replace us. I think it's gonna allow us to do what we do in a better way that we couldn't possibly get otherwise."
🌍 Running 40+ European markets plus APAC means global strategy and local nuances. Machine learning provides the backbone. The local adaptation is still manual. Nobody has cracked that at scale yet.

This is a must watch episode for anyone working in subscription, streaming, or fan engagement.

⚽ 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Just discovered: Non-League Day Turns 15
How a social media experiment became English football's most effective grassroots initiative

⚫⚪ To be honest, until a few days ago, I had never heard of Non-League Day. I came across it through a Juventus Football Club post. The club announced a collaboration with three English non-league sides that play in black and white: Maidenhead United Football Club , Chorley FC, and Barnton FC. Signed shirts sent from Turin. Barnton, nicknamed "Cheshire Juve," has fans travelling between Cheshire and the Allianz Stadium. I'm based in Turin. I'm a Torino FC fan, so Juventus news lands on my radar whether I want it to or not. This one caught my eye.

🏟️ Non-League Day: every year during an international break, fans across England are encouraged to visit their local non-league club. Pay a few quid. Have a pint. Stand close enough to hear the centre-back organising the line. Started in 2010 by QPR fan James Doe. This Saturday is the 15th edition. Nearly 1,000 clubs taking part.

📊 Last year: 149,060 spectators across Steps 1-4. 12% attendance increase. A LiveScore survey this week found 55% of professional club fans are open to attending a non-league match. 4 in 10 cannot name their local non-league club. Discovery problem.

🌍 Juventus is the second major European club to engage. Athletic Bilbao launched Euskal Non-League Day in 2023 through its Foundation. Now in its fourth edition. Close to 170 affiliated Basque clubs. The only initiative of its kind in LaLiga.

💡 Here's what surprises me. The English football pyramid is one of the most extraordinary structures in global sport. Thousands of clubs connected through promotion and relegation, from the Premier League to village football. And the top brands barely use it. The pyramid is a readymade activation platform: local reach, authentic community engagement, massive geographic spread, year-round fixtures. The kind of thing a brand strategist would design from scratch if it didn't already exist. Yet most sponsors concentrate at the top two or three tiers and ignore everything below. The pyramid is sitting there. Open for business. The industry keeps walking past it.

⚽ My son plays youth football in Turin. I wrote a children's book about this, Calcio Ribelle, where a group of kids invent their own version of football built on fair play, creativity, and inclusion. Watching what Non-League Day represents, the spirit is the same. Football as a community activity, run by people who care about the game for reasons that have nothing to do with broadcast rights or sponsorship decks.

posts.text:
🤔 Is perfectionism a strength?
Perfectionism can be a strength but it can also slow momentum, drain teams, and delay impact.
❓ How do you decide when "good enough" is better than "perfect", for yourself or your team?
My friends at the #LinkedInNewsUK team asked me to elaborate on this.

😎 My honest take: perfectionism is almost never a strength. What people call "perfectionism as a strength" is usually just high standards combined with good taste. Actual perfectionism, in the product space, is a misallocation of resources toward an abstraction. Perfection doesn't exist as a deliverable. You can't ship it, you can't measure it, and you can't iterate on it.

What you can do is right-size your effort to the moment, the user, and the stage of the product.

Right-sizing means asking: what does this feature, this release, this sprint actually need to deliver value right now? An MVP that reaches users and generates real feedback is worth more than a polished product that stays in staging for three extra months. The learning you get from contact with the market is irreplaceable. No amount of internal refinement substitutes for it.

🤔 And here's the question I keep coming back to, personally: am I improving the work or just managing my anxiety? A lot of late-stage perfectionism is about fear of judgment, not about making something better. Once I started recognizing that pattern in myself, it became easier to let things go. In product terms, that translates into teams protecting their work from scrutiny, resisting feedback, delaying launches. The anxiety is the same, just distributed across a group.

This connects to a punk ethic for professional life, something I wrote about recently on A guy with a scarf. Punk (in music) was never about waiting until you had perfect technique or the right studio or the approval of gatekeepers. It was about having something to say and putting it out there. The energy and the intent mattered more than the polish. That attitude translates directly into product work: ship it, learn from it, make the next version better. The iteration is the craft.

None of this means lowering standards.

Right-sizing is a discipline. It requires judgment about where to invest deeply (core architecture, data integrity, user trust) and where to stay lean (UI details in early stages, edge cases that affect 2% of users, internal tooling). That judgment is what separates experienced product teams from junior ones.

Perfection is comfortable to chase because it postpones the vulnerable moment of putting something into the world. Right-sizing forces you to be honest about what matters now and what can wait. That takes more courage than endless polishing.

I guess at my best I am a punk-attitude engine that aims to deliver the highest quality needed and at times surprise the client, the user, the audience with some unexpected gems.

Yessi Bello-Perez

🏏 10 things to consider about $3.4 Billion in IPL Franchise Sales

🏏 Two IPL franchises changed hands this week for a combined $3.4 billion. Royal Challengers Bangalore went to a consortium including Blackstone, David Blitzer, Aditya Birla Group, and the Times of India Group for $1.78 billion. Rajasthan Royals went to a US-led group featuring the Walmart and Ford families for $1.63 billion. My friend Vinit Mehta published a strong analysis on the sports-tech implications in his Mehtta Ventures Dubai newsletter, and I wanted to amplify it for this audience because these deals deserve attention beyond the cricket press.

Here are the 10 things to consider:
1️⃣ 🏏 The valuation multiples (16x and 25x on 2008 bids) reflect NFL-level scarcity with only 10 IPL teams
2️⃣ 💰 Blackstone's first-ever sports investment landed in cricket, and David Blitzer added IPL to a portfolio spanning the NBA, NFL, NHL, MLB, EPL, and MLS
3️⃣ 🌍 Cricket has entered the global sports asset class conversation for real. Western investors can no longer treat it as a regional story
4️⃣ 📊 BCCI posted a ₹3,358 crore surplus in FY25 and is projecting ₹6,728 crore for FY26. The IPL media rights deal alone was worth $6.2 billion
5️⃣ 🚀 Indian sports-tech startups like Stupa Sports Analytics and Str8bat are positioned to benefit directly as franchise owners invest in analytics, fan engagement, and performance tech
6️⃣ 📺 The 2025 IPL final drew 169 million TV viewers. Any fan engagement technology proving itself in cricket has a market size argument that dwarfs most European football deployments
7️⃣ 🔄 The 2027+ media rights cycle becomes the real accelerator, and these franchise sales give BCCI serious ammunition
8️⃣ 🇺🇸 Cross-pollination between US sports ownership and cricket is accelerating through shared ownership networks. Vendor introductions follow ownership connections
9️⃣ ⚠️ Risks are real: high multiples, regulatory shifts (the 2025 Online Gaming Act already reshaped the sponsorship landscape), and the usual hype cycle dangers
🔟 🧭 If you work in sports media and technology, you need an India thesis. You also need to deeply understand the market before making any moves

🤖 AI, Content, and the Future of Work: Three Pieces of Thinking That Won't Leave My Head

Sports media and technology is what I do. Broadcasting, streaming, data, fan engagement. Every week I write about this industry for A Guy With A Scarf. I like my lane.

🧠 But AI is reshaping things well beyond our corner. And lately, three very different pieces have been circling in my head. They come from macro-economics, strategic foresight, and creator economy. They all land on the same question: what happens when the relationship between AI, human work, content, and value gets renegotiated all at once?
1️⃣📉 The Citrini Report ("The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis") — a scenario analysis that went viral, rattled markets, and drew responses from Citadel Securities and the White House. It describes AI-driven white-collar displacement triggering a feedback loop with no brake. The doom scenario feels excessive to me. The cascading logic behind it does not.
2️⃣🌀 Amy Webb's Convergence Outlook (SXSW 2026) — she retired her 18-year-old trend report and replaced it with a framework built on convergences: what happens when AI, labor, biotech, capital, and behavior all collide at the same time. The rebranding is partly positioning. The underlying idea, that we can no longer track these forces in isolation, is genuinely useful.
3️⃣🎵 Jack Conte's keynote (SXSW 2026) — the Patreon co-founder placed AI in the long arc of creative destruction and named the current moment the "slop phase." Then landed a sharp point: AI companies claim fair use on creators' work while signing multimillion-dollar licensing deals with Disney and Condé Nast. If it's legal to just use it, why pay anyone?

⚽ My brain keeps dragging all of this into sports media territory. What does cascading displacement mean for the thousands of knowledge workers in broadcasting, production, and analytics? What does the convergence lens mean for how we think about AI tools, automated content, and data rights as one system? What does selective fair use mean for sports organizations sitting on massive content libraries?

I don't have a finished take. I have a growing list of questions and I'd get further with other people in the room.

🏈 📺 10 things to consider About the NFL Media Rights Renegotiation
I started working with the NFL in 2016. What began as a professional engagement turned into something closer to a personal fascination. Their media rights structure is one of the most sophisticated constructions in global sports.
Right now the league is renegotiating deals worth $10 billion a year, with a target closer to $18-20 billion. All before the 2026 season starts in September.
I know this is a US-centric topic but I always felt that, even if that does not apply to other markets as-is and the NFL is so much bigger than anything else, there are lot of rationales to learn from there.

Here are the 10 things to consider👇
1️⃣ The NFL is renegotiating deals that don't expire for another seven years
2️⃣ Paramount goes first because the NFL has specific leverage over them
3️⃣ The cost-per-viewer-hour argument is the analytical engine of the process
4️⃣ The ESPN equity deal is the structural foundation for everything else

🤖 ⚙️ What a Former LinkedIn Insider Says About the 2026 Algorithm (and What 279 Comments Reveal)

I almost scrolled past it. A LinkedIn post about the LinkedIn algorithm is usually content I skip on principle. But this one had 279 comments, and Dani Markovits wrote it, he spent four years at LinkedIn, he knows how the platform works from the inside. So I stopped.

I'm stubbornly committed to writing for people, not for algorithms. I get criticized for it regularly. But I work with clients in sports media and technology who ask me about these things, so understanding what's happening under the hood matters.

I aggregated everything he wrote in the post and in his comment replies into a single view. The key points:

→ Your profile is now a ranking signal. Headline, About section, career history are context tags the algorithm reads before distributing your content.

→ Comments carry roughly 15x more weight than likes. A thoughtful comment means someone paused and engaged. A like barely registers.

→ Dwell time and saves now heavily influence distribution. Someone saving your post signals lasting value.

→ Content is matched to your demonstrated expertise. Consistency in a topic builds compounding visibility.

→ External links won't kill a post if the content earns engagement first. Essential link: include it. Optional: put it in comments.

→ Personal profiles have stronger organic reach than company pages because they're built on trust signals.

My take: Markovits brings insider credibility and clear communication, and that combination is what made the post travel. Whether the underlying information is as groundbreaking as the engagement suggests is a separate question. The 360Brew paper has been around since 2025. Dwell time has been discussed for years.

The point I'm least comfortable with is the expertise-matching logic. I have multiple identities on LinkedIn. I write about sports media, music, photography, Turin's cultural life. We live in an era of expert-generalists. If the algorithm penalizes human escapes from core competence, it's solving for a version of professional identity that is increasingly outdated. I'd hope a system with "360" in its name would try to build a full picture of who someone is.

I went through most of the 279 comments. The reactions break down roughly like this:

~15% welcomed the changes as overdue
~12% asked clarifying questions
~10% were critical of LinkedIn itself
~10% shared niche content strategies
~9% jumped into profile optimization tactics
~8% challenged the accuracy of the claims
~8% flagged concerns about AI-generated content
~6% brought humor and meta-awareness
~4% raised diversity and multi-expertise concerns
~18% left generic praise or tagged colleagues

Make LinkedIn Better for Creators

🔟 ⚽ 10 things to consider about the FIFA YouTube deal
Just saw the news last night, and started to do a bit of research. I fell asleep on it, so after breakfast and kids in school, here they are: 10 things to consider.

I read the FIFA and YouTube press releases line by line, cross-referenced with the TikTok deal from January, and checked every claim against the official sources.

Worth stating clearly from the start: YouTube has no match rights. All live match content flows through existing Media Partners on their own YouTube channels. The deal has three components: Media Partner provisions (10-minute live streams, select full matches, highlights, Shorts), a global creator program, and FIFA's Digital Archive on FIFA's own YouTube channel.

1️⃣ What the YouTube deal actually says. Three components, and how many full matches will stream remains undefined.
2️⃣ "Preferred Platform" is a specific FIFA category. YouTube is the second to receive it, TikTok was first in January.
3️⃣ What the TikTok deal actually says. "Parts of matches" with no minutes specified, no full match streaming mentioned.
4️⃣ Both deals enhance broadcaster value. The 10-minute stream is a promotional tool, not a rights transfer.
5️⃣ Creator programs are central to both deals. YouTube's language is aspirational, TikTok's is more operationally specific.
6️⃣ YouTube's scale explains the deal. 2.7 billion monthly users, every format, every screen type.
7️⃣ The Digital Archive is underreported. Full-length historical matches on FIFA's own channel, separate from the Media Partner provisions.
8️⃣ TikTok's US regulatory history adds context. FIFA announced TikTok as Preferred Platform two weeks before the divestiture deal closed.
9️⃣ IP protection runs through both agreements. YouTube has Content ID, TikTok committed to anti-piracy policies. The mechanisms differ.
🔟 The facts beyond the noise. What we know, what remains undefined, and why the open questions matter.

🔟 10 things to consider About 10 things to consider
The framework behind the format
You may have noticed that I keep writing these "10 things to consider" pieces. You may not have. Either way, I want to explain what they are and why I keep doing them.
Any numbered format carries a risk. It can slide into listicle territory, or start sounding like clickbait. I am aware of that risk every time I publish one. The reason I keep using the format is that I needed a framework to organize how I react to things that happen in our industry. When a deal drops, or a report lands, or a league makes a move, my head fills up fast. The "10 things" structure forces me to slow down, select what actually matters, and think about each aspect separately before putting it all together.
Every time I sit down to write one, the discipline is the same. I have to curate. I have to decide what makes the cut and what stays out. I have to find ten angles that are each worth the reader's time, and I have to make sure they connect into something coherent. That process challenges me every single time. Some pieces come together in a few hours. Others take days of reading, cross-referencing, and rewriting before the ten feel right.
I trusted the format enough to build an entire book around it. "Becoming a Better B2B Tech Vendor in Sports and Media" is 51 lists of 10 things to consider, organized across 10 categories. That is 510 items drawn from almost four decades on the vendor side of this industry. If the framework had felt thin or gimmicky after the first few articles, I would never have committed 200 pages to it.
I am not sure the format works for everyone. I do know it works for me as a thinking tool. It keeps me focused, it keeps me honest about what I actually understand, and it stops me from writing the kind of vague commentary that sounds smart and says nothing.

⚽ 🤖 SportsInnovation 2026: 3D Data Across Analytics, Officiating, and Fan Experience
Fourth time at SportsInnovation in Düsseldorf. This year I moderated two sessions on the main stage, both on 3D data in football. A live match was running on the pitch throughout. I have been involved in football data since 1994 and this felt like a day where things clicked into place.

🎙️  Opening session: Connected Future Ahead — Unlocking the Power of 3D Data in Football
With Hendrik Weber (DFL / Bundesliga), Christian Holzer (Sportec Solutions AG Solutions), Nicolas Evans (FIFA), John Shepherd  (EA SPORTS).

Three things that stood out:

1. Hendrik Weber compared 3D data today to tracking data fifteen years ago, when nobody knew what to do with it. The market matured, sports data became essential. 3D data is at the same tipping point now, and DFL chose to open the event with it for that reason.

2. The live automated event detection engine was processing the match in real time on screen. Christian Holzer showed how skeletal tracking identifies every touch and classifies events through ML. For the 2026 World Cup, Nicolas Evans confirmed FIFA will automate everything that is objectively automatable. Around seven top-level events will still need human judgment.

3. John Shepherd presented Project Assist: live TRACAB volumetric data combined with the Frostbite engine. The demo rendered the match on the pitch in real time with new camera angles, tactical overlays, and prediction mechanics. The hardware is already installed in all 36 Bundesliga stadiums.

🎙️ Afternoon session: Beyond the Whistle — The Future of Officiating Technology
With Nicolas Evans (FIFA) and Peter Irwin (Hawk-Eye Innovations).

Three things that stood out:

1. The Football Technology Centre is a joint venture between FIFA and Hawk-Eye designed to break the innovation deadlock. For years, vendors would say "we think it's possible, but will you guarantee us it will be used?" The joint venture is the structural answer: shared risk, shared investment, longer horizon.

2. Advanced SAOT sends the offside alert directly to the on-field referee in real time, bypassing the VAR for a high majority of cases. Peter Irwin described four to five years of edge case testing. One failure destroys trust in the entire system. That is why full automation is still ahead.

3. Any IP developed within the Football Technology Centre is licensable by any company. That was a non-negotiable condition from FIFA. When SAOT launched, Hawk-Eye was the only provider. Now there are three. Nicolas put it simply: you cannot democratize a product that does not exist.

🎙️ Ep. 79: Cyprien Castanedo - Why the First Season Is a Retention Lab, Not Just a Subscriber Count

For this episode of Retention Zone I spoke with Cyprien Castanedo, Head of Media Platform & Innovation at LFP Media, about what happens when a football league goes from selling broadcast rights to selling subscriptions directly to fans. Ligue 1 Plus launched in two months, from zero subscribers, and is now six months into one of the most fascinating D2C experiments in European sports media.

Here are the key retention takeaways 👇

1️⃣ 🤝 Trust before transactions. French fans had been through the MediaPro collapse and DAZN disappointment. Aggressive pricing was not just a commercial choice, it was a trust-rebuilding strategy.

2️⃣ 📺 Hybrid distribution beats pure OTT. Ligue 1 Plus lives on streaming, linear TV, and telco partners. In European markets like France, Italy, and Belgium, you need to meet fans where they already are.

3️⃣ 📊 Retention follows the football calendar. Subscriber spikes come with the big games. The real work is what happens after: CRM, notifications, storytelling that keeps fans engaged between matchdays.

4️⃣ ⚽ Sporting results drive churn. When Marseille's title hopes faded, LFP shifted the narrative to Champions League qualification. Retention in football means adapting your messaging to what is happening on the pitch, week by week.

5️⃣ 🧪 A/B testing is the missing piece. LFP has the data to see where people drop off in the subscription flow, but not yet the flexibility to experiment fast enough. Full A/B testing capability is a top priority for season two.

6️⃣ 💳 Involuntary churn adds up. Failed payments, expired cards, banking issues. Small percentage gains in payment recovery compound into significant subscriber retention over a full season.

7️⃣ 🤖 AI as advisor first, autopilot later. Cyprien wants AI to surface insights and flag at-risk subscribers, but giving it full autonomy on retention offers risks fairness issues that one social media post can turn into a trust problem.

8️⃣ 🔄 The org shift matters most. Going from B2B to B2C in two months meant learning e-commerce, consumer marketing, and CRM from scratch. Cyprien called this agility "maybe the number one success element on the project."

The first season is not just about counting subscribers. It is a retention lab. And season two is already in the works.

10 things to consider
⚽ 📲 The League Buys the Game Inside the Game
How Lega Serie A's €18 million acquisition of Fantacalcio.it gave Italian football its first direct relationship with three million fans.

Last Monday in Milan, the Lega Serie A voted to acquire 51% of Quadronica Srl — the Naples-based company behind Fantacalcio.it, Italy's dominant fantasy football platform. Fifteen clubs said yes. Three said no. Two abstained. The full company was valued at just under €40 million. The deal is financed by a self-liquidating loan repaid through Fantacalcio's own profits. The clubs spend nothing upfront.
Most coverage filed it as Italian football diversifying its revenues. I think it is considerably more than that.

I wrote the full analysis for my A guy with a scarf Untangling series. Here are the ten things worth considering:
1️⃣ The Lega just acquired the largest authenticated fan database in Italian football, and it did not have to build it.
2️⃣ The deal structure tells you as much about Italian football governance as the deal itself.
3️⃣ The three clubs that voted no share something more interesting than a view on the price.
4️⃣ Fantacalcio's advertising model is quietly more sophisticated than most sports sponsorship inventory.
5️⃣ The founders staying is the single most important detail in the entire deal.
6️⃣ The real risk is not that the Lega will charge for the app. The real risk is that the app starts to feel like the Lega made it.
7️⃣ The Lega now has the infrastructure — on paper — to consider what managing its own broadcasting looks like.
8️⃣ Private equity came calling more than once. Ragosta and Cutolo said no every time.
9️⃣ In 2025, Fantacalcio produced its own scripted web series and attracted a Netflix feature film. The Lega bought a company that was already becoming a media company.
🔟 Ninety percent market share built over twenty-five years by two guys from Naples who started with a website for their friends. That is not a metric. That is a relationship.
