⚽ Football Through Their Eyes - A Multidimentional Experience
🏃‍♂️‍➡️ What Three Ten-Year-Olds Taught Me About the Sport I Thought I Knew

A personal post. Observing my son relationship with football and applying a bit of my distorted sport and media glasses, I noticed that his approach has a wide 360 degrees view on the sport.

It's not only like we said in the past "play and watch" or "viewers/participants", it's a more multidimensional experience.

So as friends were visiting this weekend I took 15 minutes of their playing time and sit them done for a recorded audio interview based on a set of questions.
My angle was no to telkl a story of kids in football (I wrote a fun novel about that) but to grab insights for our industry.

They told me the why, how and what of football in their lives - quite a significant footprint at this age.
What came out is an experience that includes:
⚽ Playing on the pitch (5 days a week)
- Training, matches, teammates, routines, and the physical feeling of the game. The centre of the ecosystem.
⚽ Watching football
- Live matches, highlights, and moments shared at home that extend what happens on the field.
⚽ Digital football and Gaming
- EA FC sessions where tactics, players, and imagination continue the experience between real games.
⚽ Physical games
 Subbuteo, tabletop football, and small tactile recreations that keep the game present away from screens.
⚽ Invented football
- Calciomercato, Fantacalcio, Fields drawn with a pen on paper, improvised rules, games created from imagination and friendship.
⚽ Collecting and stickers
 Panini albums, trading duplicates, discovering teams and players through images and memory.
⚽ Stadium experience
- Atmosphere, chants, sensory moments, and shared emotional release.
⚽ Social football
- Conversations at school and training, jokes, debates, and shared language before social media fully enters their lives.
⚽ Everyday micro-moments
- Small rituals, spontaneous discussions, and tiny gestures that keep football alive throughout the week.

Consider the age - these kids do not have access to social yet - teenagers will have a different multidimensional experience shape.

The clearing, not the end 🗺️

Viewing behaviour changes faster than the rules used to describe it.

posts.text:
🙌🏼 📲 Khaby Lame isn’t Exiting. He Is Re-Positioning and Going Public

😵 I don’t usually react to misinterpreted news on LinkedIn. But this time the superficiality was hard to ignore.
😱 Most coverage missed the central point.
Khaby Lame comes from Chivasso, just outside Torino, where I’ve lived my whole life. That proximity alone made me look twice at the recent headlines about his “exit”.
❌ This was not an exit.
✅  It was an all-stock deal.

🏦 Khaby Lame merged his operating company into the Nasdaq-listed Rich Sparkle in an all-stock deal, becoming a controlling shareholder, with no cash exit and his future value now tied to public market performance.

Here’s what actually matters 👇
💵  Was this a cash deal?
 No. It was share-for-share. No big cheque, just equity in a public company.
💵 Does the $900m+ number mean money earned?
 No. It’s a valuation reference, not cash in the bank.
💵 Did Khaby sell everything?
 No. He owned 49% of the operating company. Outcomes are proportional.
💵 Did this reduce his risk?
 No. It increased exposure. His future is now tied to public market performance.
💵 Why go public this way?
 Because merging into an already listed company is a shortcut to market visibility, without a traditional IPO.
One more thing most people skipped: this makes Khaby a controlling shareholder in a Nasdaq-listed entity, with governance, disclosure, and investor pressure that creators rarely face.

This is not a fairytale ending.
 It’s a repositioning, from platform-native creator growth to public-market scrutiny.

I wrote a long-form piece breaking this down calmly and structurally, including why Rich Sparkle matters and why this pattern keeps appearing in the creator economy.
This story is about what the creator economy is becoming when it runs out of simple paths forward.

 Monthly plans now sit alongside passes, seasons, pay-per-view, and platform bundles. More choice, more complexity, direct impact on retention.

 Automated outreach is saturated. Preparation, relevance, referrals, and real conversations cut through.

 Smoother, more secure, more local. When payments work, users forget them. When they fail, retention drops.

 Retention is no longer a funnel metric.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
😵 😱 🥰 Permacrisis: Is sport the ultimate drama queen?

🥇 For a long time, the sports industry operated in a protected environment. Revenues felt structurally secure, media rights sat at the centre, and long cycles created a sense of permanence. Stability became an assumption.
That assumption has been eroding slowly. Not through collapse, but through friction. Renewals take longer. Margins tighten unevenly. Outcomes become less predictable. Some positions that once felt guaranteed no longer are.

⚽ In that environment, urgency starts to shape everything. Decisions arrive framed as unavoidable. Change accelerates. Emergency language becomes normal. This condition has been described clearly in a recent Future Proof News Nick Hilton's article on permacrisis, which gave a name to something many people recognise intuitively.

🏈 I found that framing useful, and it pushed me to write my own piece. Not to repeat the argument, but to look at how permacrisis shows up in everyday decision-making, language, and behaviour across sport.

😎 I am not outside this dynamic. I have worked for years helping a conservative industry engage with innovation as it arrived. That meant encouraging openness, experimentation, and curiosity. Working in that space also meant living close to urgency, and absorbing some of its language along the way.

🎾 The question worth asking now concerns emphasis. How often calm and judgment were reinforced while organisations were being encouraged to open themselves to change.
My article is an attempt to slow the conversation down, name the pattern, and create space to think with more solid rationales. Or should we?

Thanks to Jen Topping, Richard Gillis and Unofficial Partner

🤖 Why memory, not intelligence, is becoming the real retention engine of AI 🤖
The AI That Remembers You Is the AI You Don’t Want To Leave
Retention Zone Exclusive

I think I've discovered why I can't leave my main AI tool. And it's not what you'd expect.
Over the past year, I've been using dozens of AI platforms for my work as a media tech advisor. Some are faster, some are smarter, some excel at specific tasks.
But without planning it, I realized I'd started treating one platform completely differently. It became "home" while the others became utilities.

🤖 The reason wasn't price or performance. It was memory.

Not marketing-speak memory, but real accumulated context. This system learned how I work, which voice I use for different projects, the rules I set once and don't want to repeat daily. It remembered that I switch between 4-5 distinct personas throughout the day.
That made a difference. The AI stopped feeling like a vending machine and started feeling like a workspace where my effort accumulates rather than evaporates.

Here's what struck me: Traditional retention tactics (onboarding flows, notifications, pricing bundles) feel primitive compared to this. Memory creates retention without trying. You don't decide to stay – you simply stop considering leaving.
I think we're seeing the emergence of a hub-and-spoke model: one "home" AI that knows your context, surrounded by utility tools for specific tasks.

But here's my confession: This is based entirely on my personal experience. I obsess over retention for subscription services, but I'm essentially a sample size of one here. The data isn't in yet.
Questions for the community:
🤖 Are you experiencing this "home AI" pattern too?
🤖 Have you noticed yourself getting attached to one platform over others?
🤖 If so, what's driving that attachment?

I wrote about this extensively in the article below because I think other subscription services could learn from AI's accidental discovery that retention often comes from remembering better, not adding more features.
But I could be completely wrong.
What's your experience been?

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
🤖 I got distracted by agentic AI hype and, to be honest, I’ve become quite skeptical about its immediate value.
That’s probably partly my fault, and partly the lack of truly convincing, everyday use cases I see around me. Lots of demos, lots of promises, not enough clear “this changed how we work” 🤨 stories, but also some quite negative media coverage.
So I was ready to dismiss most of it.
Then I read the latest Claude report on AI agents and thought, ok, maybe I’m being too harsh. Or at least too impatient.

A few things stood out for me:
🤖 Over half of the companies surveyed are already using agents for multi-step workflows, and a meaningful share for processes that cut across teams. 🤨
🤖 Coding is where agents are already boringly effective. Close to everyone uses them, mostly in production, not experiments. Time saved is spread across planning, writing, testing, documentation. That matters. 🤫
🤖 The next wave is less glamorous but more real: research, reporting, data analysis, internal process automation. The work nobody brags about on stage, but everyone needs done. 🦾
🤖 Most teams don’t go “all in” or “DIY everything”. They mix off-the-shelf agents with custom pieces where it really counts. That feels very enterprise-real. 😎
🤖 The most interesting signal: many organisations say they’re already seeing measurable ROI. Not projected value, not pilots. Actual impact, mostly through speed and efficiency gains.
❓ Will they perform long term?

What this report did not magically give me is a killer, universal agentic use case. But it did reframe things.
Agentic AI seems to work best when:
🤖 the task is well defined,
🤖 context is available,
🤖  integration is taken seriously,
🤖  and humans are willing to redesign workflows, not just bolt tools on top.

I’m still skeptical about sweeping claims.
Happy to be proven wrong. Or right. Either way, this one is worth reading.

The The Wall Street Journal recently published an article (Katie Deighton) with a telling signal.
Companies are increasingly hiring for roles explicitly called “storyteller.”
The piece reads as a labour-market indicator. As organisations grow more complex and communication happens continuously and in public, narrative ownership is becoming a structural function rather than a side activity.

I spent 35 years inside the same company, across technology, product, partnerships, and innovation roles. None of my job titles included storytelling. Maintaining coherence as initiatives moved from idea to launch.
I was also in a particularly fortunate position. I was often involved/driving, from early, strategy shaping through idea generation and into product launches. That continuity made it easier to speak with accuracy and restraint.
Only later did I realise how much that interpretive layer mattered.

If I were CEO of a B2B tech vendor in the sports, media and entertainment ecosystem in 2026, I would focus on three things.

Clients do not buy stacks. They buy reduced risk, saved time, and measurable impact.

Procurement friction, integration fear, and internal alignment kill more deals than competitors ever will.

Serving everyone usually means building for no one. Focus is not a constraint, it is a signal.

Move to cancellable, outcome-based commitments.

How buying decisions are actually made inside sports and media organisations, beyond job titles.

🤖 Retention Zone, Wrapped 2025
I went back through every Retention Zone conversation from this year and pulled out what really stayed with me more.
Not trends.
Not buzzwords.
Actual sentences said by people who operate this stuff every day.

A few of them say more about retention than a hundred slides:
🎙️ John-Paul McKerlie
“You can have the best product in the world, but if paying is painful, customers will leave.”
🎙️ Tom Burrell
“Retention doesn’t happen everywhere. It happens in very specific moments that really matter. Moments of truth.”
🎙️ Kübra Güven
“A lot of churn issues come from teams (content, marketing, product, tech) not being aligned internally.”
🎙️ Motasem El Bawab
“Retention is a mindset. It’s how the organisation thinks and behaves, not just a number on a dashboard.”
🎙️ Gilles Domartini
“If AI just gives you more dashboards, it doesn’t help. It has to help people take decisions.”

That’s the year, summed up better than I ever could.
Huge thanks to everyone who joined Retention Zone in 2025, on the show and at Retention Zone LIVE in Amsterdam. More conversations ahead.
See you in 2026.

🤖 💶 🇮🇹 ⚽ Tether, Juventus and the Italian Idea of Ownership

I live in Turin. My football heart is granata — Toro — but when something shakes Juventus, it inevitably shakes the whole city.
So I wrote a long-form piece on the Tether bid, the Agnelli response, and what this moment really tells us about ownership, identity and the economics of Italian football.

And yes, there’s a moment of Turin irony: the Agnelli family built FIAT, while Tether issues fiat-backed stablecoins… somewhere out there a confused strategy deck probably merged the two, with a ChatGPT hallucination whispering “perfect alignment” for an investment in football. #joke

Here’s what you’ll find in the article:
➡️ The Italian view from inside Turin, even from the Toro side of town
➡️ What Tether actually is — and why its Juventus bid was serious
➡️ Why Exor’s “no” wasn’t financial, but cultural and structural
➡️ How Juventus’s valuation compares to other top clubs
➡️ The emerging context: Exor selling its newspaper group, Cairo’s dual role, and why people connect dots
➡️ A full media review with literal quotes from Corriere, Repubblica, La Stampa, Tuttosport, Gazzetta, Il Sole

⚽ 🇮🇹 What's going on between DAZN and Serie A?
In Italy everyone is talking about DAZN and Lega Serie A again, but this time it’s not about latency, piracy or production quality.
It’s about equity.

Over the last few days, Milano Finanza, Calcio e Finanza and others have reported two parallel hypotheses being explored:
1️⃣ A small equity stake in DAZN Group for Lega Serie A, “sul modello NFL”
2️⃣ A 10% swap of TV money into DAZN shares for some clubs, starting with those owned by funds
I try to do one thing clearly: separate what the Italian media actually report from what is still financial fiction.

I go through:
➡️ The numbers and language used by Milano Finanza, Calcio e Finanza, TiVuBiz, Business People, etc...
➡️ How the 2024–29 DAZN/Sky deal really works today (fixed fees + revenue share)
➡️ What changes if clubs start converting part of those guaranteed cheques into equity
➡️ Why everyone keeps citing the “NFL model”, and why the NFL–ESPN deal is not the same thing as what’s on the table in Italy

As always, the interesting part is not the headline rumour but the second-order effects: governance, conflicts of interest, valuation risk, and what this says about the future relationship between leagues and platforms.

If you work in sport, media or private equity, this one is worth a careful read.
